citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $M$ be a smooth four-manifold without boundary, so that $M$ is Hausdorff
and second countable and carries a maximal smooth atlas
([[def-smooth-manifold]]). Let $g$ be a smooth covariant $2$-tensor field on $M$
in the sense of [[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]]. Then $g$ assigns
to every $p\in M$ a bilinear form $g_p:T_pM\times T_pM\to\mathbb R$
([[def-derivation-at-a-point-and-tangent-space]]).

**(a) Lorentzian metric.** The field $g$ is a **Lorentzian metric of signature
$(-,+,+,+)$** on $M$ when it is symmetric and nondegenerate, and at every
$p\in M$ the pair $(T_pM,g_p)$ is a Lorentz vector space of signature
$(-,+,+,+)$ in the sense of [[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]: that is, $g_p$ has
inertia $(3,1,0)$, so that some — equivalently every — basis of $T_pM$ in which
the matrix of $g_p$ is diagonal has exactly one negative and three positive
diagonal entries. The pair $(M,g)$ is a **smooth Lorentzian four-manifold** (or
Lorentzian manifold of signature $(-,+,+,+)$). In a smooth chart $(U,x)$ the
**components** of $g$ are the $C^\infty$ functions
$g_{ab}(q)=g_q(\partial_a|_q,\partial_b|_q)$ of
[[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]], and $g_{ab}=g_{ba}$ by symmetry.
We use indices $a,b,c,d=0,1,2,3$ and the Einstein summation convention, with
components in a chart written as lower-case indexed symbols and equations
between indexed fields understood basis-independently. These conventions are
fixed once for this library and the physical reading of the symbols is recorded
with the framework postulates, separately from this mathematical definition.

**(b) Pointwise causal structure.** For every $p\in M$ the vocabulary of
[[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]] applies to the Lorentz vector
space $(T_pM,g_p)$: a tangent vector $v\in T_pM$ is **timelike** when
$g_p(v,v)<0$, **null** when $v\neq0$ and $g_p(v,v)=0$, **spacelike** when
$g_p(v,v)>0$, and **causal** when it is timelike or null. Every nonzero
$v\in T_pM$ has exactly one causal character. The **timelike set**
$T_p:=\{v\in T_pM:g_p(v,v)<0\}$ has exactly two connected components, each
nonempty, open, convex and path-connected; each $g_p$-orthonormal basis
$e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3$ of $T_pM$ satisfies $g_p(e_a,e_b)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$
for some ordering, so in particular nonzero orthonormal vectors exist at every
point ([[lem-lorentz-form-has-orthonormal-basis]],
[[lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components]]).

**(c) Time orientation.** A **time orientation** of $(M,g)$, also called a
**choice of future cone**, is a smooth vector field $N$ on $M$
([[def-smooth-vector-field-as-a-tangent-bundle-section]], whose tangent-bundle
smooth structure uses the axiom $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ of
[[def-countable-choice]]; this is the only use of that axiom in this
definition) such that

$$g_p(N_p,N_p)<0\qquad\text{for every }p\in M .$$

The function $p\mapsto g_p(N_p,N_p)$ is $C^\infty$ because $g$ is a smooth
covariant $2$-tensor field and $N$ a smooth field, so the condition is a
pointwise strict inequality between a smooth function and $0$; since
$g_p(N_p,N_p)<0$ implies $N_p\neq0$, a time orientation is nowhere vanishing.
A **time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold** is a triple $(M,g,N)$
consisting of a smooth Lorentzian four-manifold and a time orientation $N$.

Given a time orientation $N$ and $p\in M$, the vector $N_p$ is timelike, and we
**define** a nonzero causal vector $v\in T_pM$ to be **future-directed** when
$g_p(v,N_p)<0$ and **past-directed** when $g_p(v,N_p)>0$. The classification of
nonzero causal vectors into exactly these two classes, and its agreement with
the two components of the timelike set (the future component is the component
$C_p^+$ containing $N_p$, and the future causal vectors form
$\operatorname{cl}(C_p^+)\setminus\{0\}$), is proved in
[[lem-gr-future-causal-classification-by-a-timelike-field]]; in particular no
nonzero causal $v$ satisfies $g_p(v,N_p)=0$, so the definition is exhaustive and
mutually exclusive. Replacing $N$ by $-N$ reverses every future/past label, and
two time orientations $N,N'$ determine the same future-directed causal vectors
at every point where $g_p(N_p,N'_p)<0$, while they determine opposite ones
where $g_p(N_p,N'_p)>0$, by
[[lem-gr-timelike-fields-define-equal-or-opposite-future-cones]]; that lemma
also shows the sign of $p\mapsto g_p(N_p,N'_p)$ is constant on every connected
component of $M$.

**(d) The inverse metric.** Because $g_p$ is nondegenerate, it induces at each
$p$ an isomorphism $\flat_p:T_pM\to T_p^*M$, $v\mapsto g_p(v,\cdot)$, and an
inverse metric $g_p^{-1}$ on the dual space; the inverse metric, the musical
isomorphisms and the components $g^{ab}$ are defined separately on this page,
where the smoothness of those components is also proved. Neither construction
uses any choice principle beyond the one already recorded in (c).


**(e) Smooth timelike curves and their scalar normalization.** Before using
these quantities in the physical conventions, fix a positive real scaling
parameter $c$ (with no physical meaning or dimension in this mathematical
item). A **smooth future timelike curve** is a smooth map $\gamma:I\to M$
from a nonempty open real interval $I$ ([[def-interval]],
[[def-c-r-and-smooth-maps-between-smooth-manifolds]]) whose velocity derivation
$\gamma'(s)\in T_{\gamma(s)}M$
([[def-velocity-derivation-of-a-smooth-curve]]) satisfies
$g(\gamma',\gamma')<0$ and $g(\gamma',N)<0$ at every $s\in I$.
In a chart its components are $d(x^a\circ\gamma)/ds$, $a=0,1,2,3$.
For a supplied base point $s_0\in I$ and additive constant $\tau_0\in\mathbb R$
define

$$h(s):=\sqrt{-g_{\gamma(s)}(\gamma'(s),\gamma'(s))},\qquad \tau(s):=\tau_0+\frac1c\int_{s_0}^{s}h(r)\,dr,\qquad U(s):=\frac{c\gamma'(s)}{h(s)}.$$

The integral is oriented when $s<s_0$. The function $\tau$ is called
**proper time** for this scaling and $U$ the **four-velocity** of the smooth
curve; its increment times $c$ is the Lorentzian length. The well-definedness
proof below shows $\tau'>0$, that $\tau:I\to\tau(I)$ is a smooth
diffeomorphism, and that $U$ is the velocity of $\gamma\circ\tau^{-1}$.
Thus $g(U,U)=-c^2$ and $U$ is future timelike. This introduces the smooth
case before any physical unit reading; the later worldline definition extends
it to its stated $C^k$, endpoint and piecewise-$C^1$ classes. It asserts no
clock coupling, motion law or physical value of $c$.

**Convention and scope.** The physical reading of a smooth time-oriented
Lorentzian four-manifold as a classical spacetime model, and the domain in which
that reading is adopted, are recorded in the framework postulate
`post-gr-spacetime-and-classical-domain`; the words spacetime and event carry no
mathematical content beyond this definition, and this item asserts no claim
about nature. The dimension $4$ and the absence of boundary are part of the
data; nothing in the definition assumes that $M$ is nonempty or connected, and
no completeness, extendibility or maximality property of $(M,g)$ is asserted.

Use the signature $(-,+,+,+)$ throughout. In the flat case, **Minkowski spacetime** means the affine model $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ of [[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]: $A$ is an affine space, $\eta$ is a nondegenerate Lorentz form on its four-dimensional displacement space, and $C^+$ selects the future cone. In the curved case, a **background spacetime** means a prescribed smooth time-oriented Lorentzian four-manifold $(M,g,N)$ of [[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]; the metric and time orientation are fixed data, not dynamical unknowns here. No field equation or completeness assumption is included.

A **massive worldline** on an open interval $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ is a $C^2$ curve $x:I\to M$ with future-directed timelike tangent $T=dx/ds$ at every parameter value. This is the smooth subclass of [[def-gr-timelike-worldline-and-proper-time]]. A **null worldline** is a $C^2$ curve with nonzero future-directed null tangent everywhere. Its tangent has no proper-time normalization: $g(T,T)=0$, so the massive proper-time formula does not apply. In the flat model these are affine curves into $A$ with tangent in the selected future timelike or null cone from [[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]].

An **observer at an event** $p\in M$ is a future unit timelike vector $n\in T_pM$ with $g_p(n,n)=-1$, as in [[def-gr-observer-and-rest-space]]. Its instantaneous rest space is $n^\perp=\{v:g_p(v,n)=0\}$. This is a pointwise vector-space construction; the definition does not assign a clock reading or a moving frame to a lone observer.

An **observer congruence** on an open set $U\subseteq M$ is a smooth field of future unit timelike vectors on $U$, as in [[def-gr-observer-congruence-and-adapted-charts]]; its observer curves are its integral curves. A **tetrad** is a chosen orthonormal frame field, as in [[def-gr-local-frame-and-tetrad-fields]]. A **chart** is a coordinate map; an adapted chart is a chart whose spatial coordinates are constant along the congruence's integral curves. These objects are distinct: a chart need not be inertial, a tetrad need not be coordinate induced, and a congruence is a field of observers rather than a chart or a frame. This distinction agrees with [[def-sr-chart-tetrad-and-congruence-distinction]].

The coordinates and units used later are SI: in an inertial chart $x^0=ct$ and $x^i$ are metres, $t$ is seconds, $c>0$ is metres per second, and proper time is measured in seconds. In a general chart, coordinate components inherit their coordinate units; invariant equations are tensorial. No global inertial chart, global tetrad, or global observer congruence is asserted to exist.

Let $F:M^m\to N^n$ be smooth, let $q\in N$ be a regular value, and assume
$F^{-1}(q)$ is nonempty. Then $F^{-1}(q)$ is an embedded submanifold of
codimension $n$. Equivalently, it has dimension $m-n$.

Let $L(q,v)$ be $C^2$ on a conic open subset of a tangent bundle, and suppose $L(q,av)=aL(q,v)$ for every $a>0$ in its domain. At each nonzero $v$,

$$v^iL_{v^i}=L,\qquad L_{v^iv^j}v^i=0,\qquad E_L:=v^iL_{v^i}-L=0.$$

Consequently the velocity Hessian is singular and the fibre derivative cannot be a local diffeomorphism there; a regular Legendre equivalence theorem cannot be applied. These conclusions do not imply that the motion is static or that the Lagrangian has a specified constraint surface.

Let $\eta$ be a Lorentz form on a $4$-dimensional real vector space $V$. There
is an ordered basis $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of $V$ with
$\eta(e_a,e_b)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$ for all $a,b$. Such a basis
is called **$\eta$-orthonormal**; in every $\eta$-orthonormal ordered basis
exactly one basis vector is timelike and the other three are spacelike, and the
count is the inertia $(3,1,0)$ of $\eta$.

Let $c > 0$ and let $(A,V,\eta,C^{+})$ be an oriented time-oriented affine
Minkowski space ([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]).

**(a) Norm of the four-velocity.** Let $x : I \to A$ be a $C^{1}$ future
timelike worldline with four-velocity $U$
([[def-sr-four-velocity-and-four-acceleration]]). Then
$\eta(U(s),U(s)) = -c^{2}$ for every $s \in I$; equivalently the dimensionless
four-velocity $u = U/c$ satisfies $\eta(u,u) = -1$, and $U(s)$ is future
timelike. Thus the dimensionless four-velocity lies on the future unit
hyperboloid $\{v \in C^{+}:\eta(v,v)=-1\}$.

**(b) Orthogonality of the four-acceleration.** If $x$ is $C^{2}$ at $s$, then
$\eta(U(s),A(s)) = 0$: the four-acceleration has no component along the
four-velocity; if in addition $A(s) \ne 0$, then $A(s)$ is spacelike.

**(c) Rest space and projection.** Let $n \in V$ be future unit timelike,
$\eta(n,n) = -1$, and put $n^{\perp} := \{\,v \in V : \eta(n,v) = 0\,\}$
([[def-lorentz-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]]). Then $n^{\perp}$ is a
3-dimensional linear subspace of $V$, the restriction of $\eta$ to $n^{\perp}$
is positive definite, and the map $h : V \to V$, $h(v) := v + \eta(n,v)\,n$, is
linear, idempotent with $h \circ h = h$, has image $n^{\perp}$ and kernel
$\operatorname{span}(n)$, satisfies $h(n) = 0$ and $\eta(n,h(v)) = 0$ for all
$v \in V$, and every $v \in V$ has the unique decomposition
$v = -\eta(n,v)\,n + h(v)$. Moreover $|w| := \sqrt{\eta(w,w)}$ defines a norm
on $n^{\perp}$.

**(d) Relative velocity and Lorentz factor.** Let $n$ and $u$ be future unit
timelike vectors, put $\gamma := -\eta(n,u)$ and $w := c\,h(u)/\gamma$. Then
$\gamma \ge 1$, $w$ lies in $n^{\perp}$,
$u = \gamma\,(n + w/c)$, $|w|^{2} = c^{2}(1-\gamma^{-2}) < c^{2}$,
$\gamma = (1-|w|^{2}/c^{2})^{-1/2}$, and $\gamma = 1$ if and only if $u = n$.
The vector $w$ is the velocity of a worldline with four-velocity $cu$ relative
to the observer $n$, and $\gamma$ is its Lorentz factor.

**(e) Coordinate form.** Let $(o;e_0,\dots,e_3)$ be an inertial frame and let
$y$ be a $C^{1}$ future timelike worldline whose inertial coordinates are
$t \mapsto (ct,r(t))$, with coordinate velocity $w(t) := r'(t)$ in
$\mathbb{R}^{3}$ and, when $y$ is $C^{2}$, coordinate acceleration
$a(t) := w'(t)$. Then $|w(t)| < c$, the four-velocity is
$U = \gamma_w\,(c,w)$ with $\gamma_w := (1-|w|^{2}/c^{2})^{-1/2}$, and the
four-acceleration is $A = \gamma_w\,\frac{d}{dt}\bigl(\gamma_w(c,w)\bigr)$, so
that

$$A^{0} = \gamma_w^{4}\,\frac{w \cdot a}{c}, \qquad A_{\mathrm{vec}} = \gamma_w^{2}\,a + \gamma_w^{4}\,\frac{(w \cdot a)\,w}{c^{2}} ;$$

consequently
$\eta(A,A) = \gamma_w^{4}|a|^{2} + \gamma_w^{6}(w \cdot a)^{2}/c^{2} \ge 0$,
with $\eta(A,A) = 0$ if and only if $a = 0$, and $\eta(U,A) = 0$. For the
observer $n = e_0$ of the chart, clauses (c) and (d) specialize to
$\gamma = \gamma_w$ and $w_{\mathrm{rel}} = (0,w)$ in the frame coordinates, identified with $w$ via the spatial basis.

**(f) Scope.** The statement is a theorem about the affine Minkowski model with
a fixed positive constant $c$; it asserts no clock reading and identifies no
physical four-velocity. No choice principle is used.

derivations.claim: Use the supplied smooth tangent/cotangent bundle structure under [A1] and the Lorentzian data [F1]. Differentiate $L=-mc\sqrt{-g_{ij}V^iV^j}$ with respect to $V^a$. Because $s>0$, ordinary chain rule gives $p_a=mcV_a/s$. Differentiating again gives $L_{V^aV^b}=mc(g_{ab}/s+V_aV_b/s^3)$.

Contract the Hessian with $V^b$: $mc(V_a/s+V_a g(V,V)/s^3)=0$, since $g(V,V)=-s^2$. For $W\perp_g V$, contraction with $W$ has quadratic value $(mc/s)g(W,W)$. The normalized vector $u=V/s$ is future unit timelike by [F2]; [F5] identifies this tangent Lorentz space with the standard Lorentz vector space, and [F6] makes its orthogonal complement positive definite. Thus the Hessian is positive on every nonzero $W\perp_g V$, so its kernel is precisely $\mathbb RV$ and its rank is three.

The momentum in step 1.1 satisfies $g^{-1}(p,p)=(mc/s)^2g(V,V)=-m^2c^2$ and is future because it is a positive multiple of $V^\flat$. Conversely, for any future covector on this shell, set $V=p^\sharp$. Then $s=mc$, and the same formula returns $p$; every positive multiple of $V$ returns the same covector. This proves exact image and positive-ray fibres.

The defining function $C=\tfrac12(g^{-1}(p,p)+m^2c^2)$ has fibre differential $d_pC=p^\sharp\ne0$ on the shell. By [F3] the shell is embedded. The Legendre map fixes the base point and has fibre differential of rank three by step 2.1, so its differential has rank $4+3=7$, the shell dimension; it is a submersion onto that image.
Euler's identity from [F4] gives $p(V)-L=0$, while the nonzero kernel direction in step 2.1 rules out a local diffeomorphism and any four-velocity inverse.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume countable choice $\mathrm{AC}_{\omega}$: every sequence of nonempty sets has a choice function ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $Q$ be a finite-dimensional, Hausdorff, second-countable smooth manifold without boundary, of dimension $n$. Its cotangent bundle is

$$T^*Q=\coprod_{q\in Q}T_q^*Q,\qquad \pi:T^*Q\to Q,\quad \pi(q,p)=q,$$

with the canonical smooth structure and induced cotangent charts supplied by the manifold construction in [[def-tautological-one-form-on-a-cotangent-bundle]]. The **tautological one-form** is $\theta_{(q,p)}(\xi)=p(d\pi_{(q,p)}\xi)$, and the **canonical cotangent two-form** is $\omega=-d\theta$. The exact theorem [[thm-the-canonical-cotangent-two-form-is-symplectic]] makes $(T^*Q,\omega)$ a symplectic manifold in the sense of [[def-symplectic-form-and-symplectic-manifold]]. We call this pair the **cotangent phase space** of $Q$.

In an induced chart $(q^1,\ldots,q^n,p_1,\ldots,p_n)$, $\theta=p_i\,dq^i$ and $\omega=dq^i\wedge dp_i$. A mathematical **observable** on this phase space means a smooth function $F:T^*Q\to\mathbb R$; this definition does not assert that a measurement has been performed or that every such function is physically measurable.

For an interpreted particle model, assign coordinates $q^i$ their declared units and assign the conjugate covector components $p_i$ units of action divided by the units of $q^i$. Thus $\theta$ and $\omega$ have action units, conventionally joule-seconds, and a bracket of quantities with units $[F]$ and $[G]$ has units $[F][G]/(\text{action})$. These are dimensional interpretations of the model, not additional mathematical premises. The use of $\mathrm{AC}_{\omega}$ is exactly the use in the smooth cotangent-bundle suppliers; no full Axiom of Choice is used.

An **oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space** is a quadruple
$(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ with the following data. In this notation $V$ includes its
specified orientation; forgetting that orientation gives only the underlying
real vector space, not the full datum $V$ of the model.

1. A nonempty affine space $A$ over a $4$-dimensional real vector space $V$,
   with action $(p,v)\mapsto p+v$ and displacement $q-p\in V$
   ([[def-affine-space-and-displacement]]). In particular $V$ is a real vector
   space of dimension $4$.
2. A Lorentz form $\eta$ on $V$, i.e. a nondegenerate symmetric bilinear form of
   inertia $(3,1,0)$ ([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]). Its associated quadratic
   form is $q(v)=\eta(v,v)$.
3. An **orientation** of $V$: a positive ray of the determinant line
   $\Lambda^4V$, fixed once and for all
   ([[def-determinant-line-orientation-of-a-finite-dimensional-real-vector-space]]).
4. A **time orientation** $C^+$ of $(V,\eta)$: one of the two connected
   components of the timelike set $T=\{v\in V:\eta(v,v)<0\}$, the other being
   $C^-:=T\setminus C^+$ ([[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]]).

The following terminology is attached to such a quadruple.

- The elements $p$ of $A$ are the **events**; for events $p,q$ the vector
  $q-p\in V$ is the **displacement from $p$ to $q$**.
- The **interval** of $p,q\in A$ is the real number
  $I(p,q):=\eta(q-p,q-p)=q(q-p)$.
- Events $p,q$ are **timelike**, **null**, **spacelike** or **causally
  related** when the displacement $q-p$ is timelike, null, spacelike or causal
  in the sense of [[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]]; they are
  **future-related** when $q-p$ is future causal and **past-related** when
  $q-p$ is past causal in the sense of
  [[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]].

**No point of $A$ is distinguished.** For every $v\in V$ the translation
$\tau_v:A\to A$, $\tau_v(p):=p+v$, is a bijection, since it is inverse to
$\tau_{-v}$: $\tau_{-v}(\tau_v(p))=(p+v)+(-v)=p+(v-v)=p$ and symmetrically, by
the affine action axioms ([[def-affine-space-and-displacement]]). Displacements
are translation invariant, $\tau_v(q)-\tau_v(p)=q-p$, so every $\tau_v$ preserves
the interval, the causal classification of every ordered pair, and the sets
$C^+$, $C^-$ (which are subsets of $V$, independent of the point of $A$); it
changes only the labelling of points. The mathematical structure of the model is
exactly the quadruple $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$; no derived physical quantity (proper
time, four-velocity, momentum, energy, charge or any field) is part of this
definition, and all later structure of the framework (frames, charts, tensor
fields, worldlines) is built on this model.

**Well-definedness.** The affine-space definition supplies the action and the
unique displacements; the Lorentz-form definition supplies $\eta$ and its
inertia; the determinant-line definition supplies orientations; and the two
components of $T$ between which the time-orientation definition chooses exist by
the components lemma recorded in the well-definedness clause of
[[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]], which is also what makes the
names future and past causal in item 4 well defined.

In affine Minkowski space with inertial coordinates $x^0,x^i$ measured in metres and metric $\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, let $m\ge0$ and let

$$\Sigma_m^+=\{(x,p): -p_0=P^0=\sqrt{m^2c^2+|\mathbf p|^2},\ p_0<0\},$$

where $\mathbf p\ne0$ when $m=0$, and write $P^i=p_i$ for the spatial raised momentum components. The characteristic flow of the restricted canonical form is $(x,p)\mapsto(x+\alpha P,p)$, and its orbit space is globally diffeomorphic to $B_m=\mathbb R^3_a\times\mathbb R^3_p$ for $m>0$, or $\mathbb R^3_a\times(\mathbb R^3_p\setminus\{0\})$ for $m=0$, by

$$a^i=x^i-\frac{P^i}{P^0}x^0,\qquad p_i=p_i.$$

The reduced symplectic form is $da^i\wedge dp_i$. The quotient is Hausdorff and second countable and each full characteristic line meets each slice $x^0=ct$ exactly once. This is an explicit free flat quotient, not a conclusion about arbitrary first-class systems.

Let $(M,g,T)$ be a prescribed smooth time-oriented Lorentzian four-manifold with signature $(-+++)$. Work in a spacetime chart on a compact parameter interval $[a,b]$ with $a<b$; take $x,p,e$ smooth on a neighbourhood of that interval, $e>0$, $m\ge0$, and $c>0$. Select stationary triples on the future shell branch after taking the independent variations: when $m>0$, $p^\sharp$ is future timelike; when $m=0$, require $p\ne0$ and $p^\sharp$ future null. Set $C_m=\tfrac12(g^{ab}p_ap_b+m^2c^2)$ and define the first-order functional

$$I_m[x,p,e]=\int_a^b\left(p_ax'^a-eC_m(x,p)\right)d\lambda.$$

Take independent smooth variations of $p,e$ and fixed-endpoint variations of $x$. Stationarity on the chart segment is equivalent to

$$x'^a=e g^{ab}p_b,\quad p'_a=-\tfrac e2\partial_a g^{bc}p_bp_c,\quad C_m=0.$$

On the massive future branch $m>0$, these equations are equivalent to stationary paths of the mathematical square-root functional $S[x]=-mc\int_a^b\sqrt{-g(x\prime,x\prime)}\,d\lambda$ on future-timelike curves with fixed endpoints; the fibre-derivative covector is $p=mc\,x'^\flat/\sqrt{-g(x',x')}$, and proper-time gauge has $e=1/m$. For the separate nonzero future-null branch $m=0$, the equations describe a null geodesic with an arbitrary positive parameter multiplier; no proper-time parameter exists. In both cases the unparameterized path is a geodesic, and no existence or completeness claim is made.

Let $(P,\omega)$ be symplectic and let $\chi_1,\ldots,\chi_{2k}$ be smooth on an open set $U$, with $C_{ab}=\{\chi_a,\chi_b\}$ invertible at every point of $U$. Write $C^{ab}$ for its inverse and $N=\{\chi=0\}\cap U$. Then $N$ is an embedded symplectic submanifold, and the bracket

$$\{F,G\}_D=\{F,G\}-\{F,\chi_a\}C^{ab}\{\chi_b,G\}$$

is the Poisson bracket of the restricted symplectic form on $N$. It is independent of ambient extensions of $F,G$, and every $\chi_a$ is a Casimir. This is local and assumes invertibility on $U$; it does not cover singular points.

Let $Q$ be a finite-dimensional smooth manifold as in [[def-rpm-h-cotangent-phase-space]], and write its cotangent phase space in induced coordinates $(q^i,p_i)$. With $\omega=dq^i\wedge dp_i$, define $X_H$ by $\iota_{X_H}\omega=dH$ and define the Poisson bracket by $\{F,G\}:=X_G(F)$. Then

$$X_H=\frac{\partial H}{\partial p_i}\frac{\partial}{\partial q^i}-\frac{\partial H}{\partial q^i}\frac{\partial}{\partial p_i},\qquad \{F,G\}=F_{q^i}G_{p_i}-F_{p_i}G_{q^i}.$$

The bracket is coordinate independent and makes smooth functions a Poisson algebra. If $H_t$ is smooth on an open time-dependent domain $D\subset\mathbb R\times T^*Q$, each solution of $\dot z=X_{H_t}(z)$ has local uniqueness and smooth dependence on initial data and parameters; on its actual interval,

$$\frac{d}{dt}F(t,z(t))=\partial_tF+\{F,H_t\}.$$

No completeness or global flow is asserted. If $H$ is smooth, each local time-$t$ flow map preserves ω.

derivations.claim: The shell equation is $-p_0^2+|\mathbf p|^2=-m^2c^2$. Its future branch has $p_0=-\sqrt{m^2c^2+|\mathbf p|^2}$. Multiplying the positive root by $c$ gives $E=\sqrt{m^2c^4+c^2|\mathbf p|^2}$, so $p_0=-E/c$.
On the gauge $x^0=ct$, the canonical term is $p_0c+p_i\dot q^i=-E+p_i\dot q^i$. The constraint term vanishes after solving $C_m=0$, yielding the displayed reduced action.

Set $\psi=x^0-ct$. From $C_m=\tfrac12(-p_0^2+|\mathbf p|^2+m^2c^2)$ and the canonical bracket, $\{C_m,\psi\}=p_0=-P^0\ne0$. Thus the matrix for $(C_m,\psi)$ is invertible; [F5] proves the gauge slice is symplectic, and the inverse $2\times2$ matrix gives $\{q^i,p_j\}_D=\delta^i_j$ and zero spatial-spatial and momentum-momentum brackets.
Varying the reduced action with fixed spatial endpoints gives Hamilton equations $\dot q^i=\partial E/\partial p_i=c^2p_i/E$ and $\dot p_i=-\partial E/\partial q^i=0$.

In the unreduced equations (x'^i=e p_i, x'^0=e(-p_0)=eE/c); hence (dx^i/dt=x'^i/(dt/d\lambda)=c^2p_i/E), while $p_i$ is constant. Because $E/c>0$, $t$ is strictly increasing and every complete affine characteristic line meets each fixed $t$ once, also as established by [F3].

Let $\mathcal D$ be an open subset of the time-dependent tangent bundle $\mathbb R\times TQ$ of a finite-dimensional smooth manifold $Q$, and let $L:\mathcal D\to\mathbb R$ be smooth. For fixed $t$, the **fibre derivative** is the map

$$\mathbb F L(t,q,v)=(t,q,p),\qquad p(w)=\left.\frac{d}{ds}\right|_{s=0}L(t,q,v+sw),$$

as in [[def-fibre-derivative-and-legendre-transform-of-a-lagrangian]]. In induced coordinates $p_i=\partial L/\partial v^i$.

The Lagrangian is **regular** at $(t,q,v)$ when the velocity Hessian $(\partial^2L/\partial v^i\partial v^j)$ is invertible there; regularity gives only a local inverse branch. It is **hyperregular on a declared domain** when $\mathbb F L$ is a diffeomorphism from that entire domain onto an open subset of $\mathbb R\times T^*Q$.

It is **almost regular on a declared domain $\mathcal D_0\subseteq\mathcal D$** when the following are all assumed: $\mathbb F L|_{\mathcal D_0}$ has constant rank; its image $N$ is an embedded submanifold of $\mathbb R\times T^*Q$; its corestriction $\mathcal D_0\to N$ is a surjective submersion (its differential is surjective at every point); and every fibre of that corestriction is connected. These hypotheses are not consequences of singularity alone.

For a smooth Lagrangian $L:TQ\to\mathbb R$, its **fibre derivative** or
**Legendre map** is the fibre-preserving smooth map

$$\mathbb FL:TQ\to T^*Q,\qquad (\mathbb FL(q,v))(w)=\left.\frac d{ds}\right|_{s=0}L(q,v+sw).$$

In bundle coordinates it is
$\mathbb FL(q^i,v^i)=(q^i,p_i)$ with
$p_i=\partial L/\partial v^i$. This coordinate formula also shows smoothness
and that the base point $q$ is unchanged.

Let $F:M^m\to N^n$ be a smooth submersion at $p\in M$. Then there are charts
near $p$ and $F(p)$ in which the coordinate representative of $F$ is

$$ (u,v)\longmapsto u $$

near the distinguished point.

derivations.claim: A tangent vector to a fibre of $\mathbb FL$ has the form $(0,0,\delta v)$ with $L_{v^iv^j}\delta v^j=0$, since the $(t,q)$ components of $\mathbb FL$ are identity components and its $p$-variation vanishes. Differentiating $E_L$ in this direction gives $dE_L(\delta v)=v^iL_{v^iv^j}\delta v^j=0$; the $L_{v^j}\delta v^j$ terms cancel.

On a connected fibre, a smooth function whose differential vanishes is constant: it is locally constant in coordinate neighborhoods, and a locally constant function on a connected space is constant. Hence $E_L$ is constant on each fibre of $\mathbb FL$. Define $h(y)$ to be this common value for any point above $y\in N$; surjectivity gives existence, and constancy gives well-definedness and uniqueness.

For each $y\in N$, [F3] gives a smooth local section $s$ of $\mathbb FL$. On that neighborhood $h=E_L\circ s$, so $h$ is smooth. These local formulas agree on overlaps because the value is already uniquely constant on each fibre. Thus globally on $N$, $E_L=h\circ\mathbb FL$.

If it annihilates $(u,v)$, its first block equation is $Av=0$, so $v=0$; its second is $-A^Tu=0$, so $u=0$. Thus it is invertible; continuity preserves invertibility on a smaller neighborhood.
[F2] applied to the combined list makes its zero surface embedded and symplectic with the displayed Dirac bracket.

In Frobenius coordinates from [F1], use the local frame $X_{\chi_a}$ along each leaf. Its derivative on the gauge map has entries $X_{\chi_a}(\phi_b)=\{\phi_b,\chi_a\}=-A_{ab}$, so it is invertible; changing to the $s$-coordinate frame multiplies by an invertible matrix. For $r\ge1$, [F3] therefore gives a local diffeomorphism of the gauge map along each leaf.

A **symplectic form** on a smooth manifold $M$ is a smooth two-form $\omega$
such that

1. $d\omega=0$, and
2. $(T_pM,\omega_p)$ is a [[def-symplectic-vector-space|symplectic vector
   space]] for every $p\in M$.

The pair $(M,\omega)$ is a **symplectic manifold**. Thus both closedness and
pointwise nondegeneracy are required. A zero-dimensional manifold with its
zero two-form satisfies the definition.

$C^\infty(M)$, with pointwise multiplication and the symplectic Poisson
bracket, is a real Poisson algebra.

Let $F:M^m\to N^n$ be smooth, let $q\in N$ be a regular value, and assume
$F^{-1}(q)$ is nonempty. Then $F^{-1}(q)$ is an embedded submanifold of
codimension $n$. Equivalently, it has dimension $m-n$.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_{\omega}$ and let $(M^{2n},\omega)$ be a smooth symplectic manifold. A finite family of smooth functions $\chi_1,\ldots,\chi_r$ defined on an open neighborhood $U\subseteq M$ is a **regular primary constraint family** on

$$C:=\{z\in U:\chi_1(z)=\cdots=\chi_r(z)=0\}$$

when $d\chi_1(z),\ldots,d\chi_r(z)$ are linearly independent at every $z\in C$. The regular-level theorem [[thm-a-regular-level-set-is-an-embedded-submanifold]] then gives $C$ its embedded-submanifold structure and $T_zC=\bigcap_a\ker d\chi_a(z)$. For functions $F,G$ on $U$, write $F\approx G$ when $F|_C=G|_C$; thus $F\approx0$ means that $F$ vanishes on $C$, without requiring it to vanish off $C$.

Given a smooth canonical Hamiltonian $H_c$ on $U$ and multiplier functions $u^a(t)$, the **total generator** is

$$H_T(t,z):=H_c(t,z)+\sum_{a=1}^r u^a(t)\chi_a(z).$$

The functions $u^a$ are independent parameter functions; the definition does not assert that their equations determine them. If $H_c$ is an energy and $\chi_a$ has units $[\chi_a]$, then $u^a$ has units energy divided by $[\chi_a]$, so every term in $H_T$ has the same units. A later constraint, if generated by consistency, is not declared primary by this definition.

derivations.claim: If $\sum_a\lambda^a d\chi_a=0$, evaluate on each $X_{\chi_b}$. This gives $\sum_a\lambda^a C_{ba}=0$ for every $b$, so invertibility implies λ=0. The differentials are independent throughout $U$; [F3] makes each nonempty joint level embedded with tangent space $TN=\cap_a\ker d\chi_a$.

For any $F$, set $X_F^D=X_F-X_{\chi_a}C^{ab}\{\chi_b,F\}$. Then $d\chi_c(X_F^D)=\{\chi_c,F\}-C_{ca}C^{ab}\{\chi_b,F\}=0$, so it is tangent to $N$. For tangent $v$, ω$(X_F^D,v)=dF(v)$, because $d\chi_a(v)=0$.

A vector tangent to $N$ in the radical of $\omega|_N$ lies in $(TN)^\omega$, which is spanned by the independent $X_{\chi_a}$ because the annihilator of $TN$ is spanned by independent $d\chi_a$ and $\omega^\flat$ is an isomorphism. Tangency of a linear combination of these fields gives a coefficient vector annihilated by $C$, hence zero. Thus $\omega|_N$ is nondegenerate; it is closed by pullback of $d\omega=0$.

Contracting the tangent field $X_F^D$ with (dG) gives $X_F^D(G)=\{G,F\}-\{G,\chi_a\}C^{ab}\{\chi_b,F\}=\{G,F\}_D$ with the declared convention after skewness and $C^{ab}=-C^{ba}$. Since $X_F^D$ is exactly the Hamiltonian field on $N$ proved in step 2.1, the bracket is the induced symplectic Poisson bracket and obeys Jacobi by [F2] applied to the symplectic $N$. If an extension vanishes on $N$, its tangent differential vanishes, so its restricted Hamiltonian field and bracket vanish; this proves extension independence. Substitution of $F=\chi_c$ in the formula gives zero by $CC^{-1}=I$, so constraints are Casimirs.

A **temporal product chart** is a smooth coordinate map from an open product $I\times\Omega\subset\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3$ onto an open subset of $M$, with coordinates $(x^0,x^1,x^2,x^3)$. We require $x^0$ to have length units and each $x^i$ to have length units in the physical interpretation.

The chart has **lapse-shift data** $(N,\beta,h)$ when $N:I\times\Omega\to(0,\infty)$, $\beta^i:I\times\Omega\to\mathbb R$, and $h_{ij}:I\times\Omega\to\mathbb R$ are smooth, $h_{ij}=h_{ji}$, and the matrix $(h_{ij})$ is positive definite at each point, with

$$g=-N^2(dx^0)^2+h_{ij}(dx^i+\beta^i dx^0)(dx^j+\beta^j dx^0).$$

Write $h^{ij}$ for the inverse matrix. The normal field is

$$n=N^{-1}(\partial_0-\beta^i\partial_i).$$

Direct contraction gives $g(n,n)=-1$; require that $n$ is future-directed in the supplied time orientation. This field of observers is distinct from the coordinate vector $\partial_0$, which may be spacelike. The coefficients $N,\beta^i,h_{ij}$ are dimensionless when all four coordinates are in metres. This definition is local to the specified product chart; it asserts no global temporal foliation.

Let $M$ be a smooth four-manifold without boundary, so that $M$ is Hausdorff
and second countable and carries a maximal smooth atlas
([[def-smooth-manifold]]). Let $g$ be a smooth covariant $2$-tensor field on $M$
in the sense of [[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]]. Then $g$ assigns
to every $p\in M$ a bilinear form $g_p:T_pM\times T_pM\to\mathbb R$
([[def-derivation-at-a-point-and-tangent-space]]).

**(a) Lorentzian metric.** The field $g$ is a **Lorentzian metric of signature
$(-,+,+,+)$** on $M$ when it is symmetric and nondegenerate, and at every
$p\in M$ the pair $(T_pM,g_p)$ is a Lorentz vector space of signature
$(-,+,+,+)$ in the sense of [[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]: that is, $g_p$ has
inertia $(3,1,0)$, so that some — equivalently every — basis of $T_pM$ in which
the matrix of $g_p$ is diagonal has exactly one negative and three positive
diagonal entries. The pair $(M,g)$ is a **smooth Lorentzian four-manifold** (or
Lorentzian manifold of signature $(-,+,+,+)$). In a smooth chart $(U,x)$ the
**components** of $g$ are the $C^\infty$ functions
$g_{ab}(q)=g_q(\partial_a|_q,\partial_b|_q)$ of
[[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]], and $g_{ab}=g_{ba}$ by symmetry.
We use indices $a,b,c,d=0,1,2,3$ and the Einstein summation convention, with
components in a chart written as lower-case indexed symbols and equations
between indexed fields understood basis-independently. These conventions are
fixed once for this library and the physical reading of the symbols is recorded
with the framework postulates, separately from this mathematical definition.

**(b) Pointwise causal structure.** For every $p\in M$ the vocabulary of
[[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]] applies to the Lorentz vector
space $(T_pM,g_p)$: a tangent vector $v\in T_pM$ is **timelike** when
$g_p(v,v)<0$, **null** when $v\neq0$ and $g_p(v,v)=0$, **spacelike** when
$g_p(v,v)>0$, and **causal** when it is timelike or null. Every nonzero
$v\in T_pM$ has exactly one causal character. The **timelike set**
$T_p:=\{v\in T_pM:g_p(v,v)<0\}$ has exactly two connected components, each
nonempty, open, convex and path-connected; each $g_p$-orthonormal basis
$e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3$ of $T_pM$ satisfies $g_p(e_a,e_b)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$
for some ordering, so in particular nonzero orthonormal vectors exist at every
point ([[lem-lorentz-form-has-orthonormal-basis]],
[[lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components]]).

**(c) Time orientation.** A **time orientation** of $(M,g)$, also called a
**choice of future cone**, is a smooth vector field $N$ on $M$
([[def-smooth-vector-field-as-a-tangent-bundle-section]], whose tangent-bundle
smooth structure uses the axiom $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ of
[[def-countable-choice]]; this is the only use of that axiom in this
definition) such that

$$g_p(N_p,N_p)<0\qquad\text{for every }p\in M .$$

The function $p\mapsto g_p(N_p,N_p)$ is $C^\infty$ because $g$ is a smooth
covariant $2$-tensor field and $N$ a smooth field, so the condition is a
pointwise strict inequality between a smooth function and $0$; since
$g_p(N_p,N_p)<0$ implies $N_p\neq0$, a time orientation is nowhere vanishing.
A **time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold** is a triple $(M,g,N)$
consisting of a smooth Lorentzian four-manifold and a time orientation $N$.

Given a time orientation $N$ and $p\in M$, the vector $N_p$ is timelike, and we
**define** a nonzero causal vector $v\in T_pM$ to be **future-directed** when
$g_p(v,N_p)<0$ and **past-directed** when $g_p(v,N_p)>0$. The classification of
nonzero causal vectors into exactly these two classes, and its agreement with
the two components of the timelike set (the future component is the component
$C_p^+$ containing $N_p$, and the future causal vectors form
$\operatorname{cl}(C_p^+)\setminus\{0\}$), is proved in
[[lem-gr-future-causal-classification-by-a-timelike-field]]; in particular no
nonzero causal $v$ satisfies $g_p(v,N_p)=0$, so the definition is exhaustive and
mutually exclusive. Replacing $N$ by $-N$ reverses every future/past label, and
two time orientations $N,N'$ determine the same future-directed causal vectors
at every point where $g_p(N_p,N'_p)<0$, while they determine opposite ones
where $g_p(N_p,N'_p)>0$, by
[[lem-gr-timelike-fields-define-equal-or-opposite-future-cones]]; that lemma
also shows the sign of $p\mapsto g_p(N_p,N'_p)$ is constant on every connected
component of $M$.

**(d) The inverse metric.** Because $g_p$ is nondegenerate, it induces at each
$p$ an isomorphism $\flat_p:T_pM\to T_p^*M$, $v\mapsto g_p(v,\cdot)$, and an
inverse metric $g_p^{-1}$ on the dual space; the inverse metric, the musical
isomorphisms and the components $g^{ab}$ are defined separately on this page,
where the smoothness of those components is also proved. Neither construction
uses any choice principle beyond the one already recorded in (c).


**(e) Smooth timelike curves and their scalar normalization.** Before using
these quantities in the physical conventions, fix a positive real scaling
parameter $c$ (with no physical meaning or dimension in this mathematical
item). A **smooth future timelike curve** is a smooth map $\gamma:I\to M$
from a nonempty open real interval $I$ ([[def-interval]],
[[def-c-r-and-smooth-maps-between-smooth-manifolds]]) whose velocity derivation
$\gamma'(s)\in T_{\gamma(s)}M$
([[def-velocity-derivation-of-a-smooth-curve]]) satisfies
$g(\gamma',\gamma')<0$ and $g(\gamma',N)<0$ at every $s\in I$.
In a chart its components are $d(x^a\circ\gamma)/ds$, $a=0,1,2,3$.
For a supplied base point $s_0\in I$ and additive constant $\tau_0\in\mathbb R$
define

$$h(s):=\sqrt{-g_{\gamma(s)}(\gamma'(s),\gamma'(s))},\qquad \tau(s):=\tau_0+\frac1c\int_{s_0}^{s}h(r)\,dr,\qquad U(s):=\frac{c\gamma'(s)}{h(s)}.$$

The integral is oriented when $s<s_0$. The function $\tau$ is called
**proper time** for this scaling and $U$ the **four-velocity** of the smooth
curve; its increment times $c$ is the Lorentzian length. The well-definedness
proof below shows $\tau'>0$, that $\tau:I\to\tau(I)$ is a smooth
diffeomorphism, and that $U$ is the velocity of $\gamma\circ\tau^{-1}$.
Thus $g(U,U)=-c^2$ and $U$ is future timelike. This introduces the smooth
case before any physical unit reading; the later worldline definition extends
it to its stated $C^k$, endpoint and piecewise-$C^1$ classes. It asserts no
clock coupling, motion law or physical value of $c$.

**Convention and scope.** The physical reading of a smooth time-oriented
Lorentzian four-manifold as a classical spacetime model, and the domain in which
that reading is adopted, are recorded in the framework postulate
`post-gr-spacetime-and-classical-domain`; the words spacetime and event carry no
mathematical content beyond this definition, and this item asserts no claim
about nature. The dimension $4$ and the absence of boundary are part of the
data; nothing in the definition assumes that $M$ is nonempty or connected, and
no completeness, extendibility or maximality property of $(M,g)$ is asserted.

Let $(M,g,T)$ be a prescribed smooth time-oriented Lorentzian four-manifold with signature $(-+++)$. Work in a spacetime chart on a compact parameter interval $[a,b]$ with $a<b$; take $x,p,e$ smooth on a neighbourhood of that interval, $e>0$, $m\ge0$, and $c>0$. Select stationary triples on the future shell branch after taking the independent variations: when $m>0$, $p^\sharp$ is future timelike; when $m=0$, require $p\ne0$ and $p^\sharp$ future null. Set $C_m=\tfrac12(g^{ab}p_ap_b+m^2c^2)$ and define the first-order functional

$$I_m[x,p,e]=\int_a^b\left(p_ax'^a-eC_m(x,p)\right)d\lambda.$$

Take independent smooth variations of $p,e$ and fixed-endpoint variations of $x$. Stationarity on the chart segment is equivalent to

$$x'^a=e g^{ab}p_b,\quad p'_a=-\tfrac e2\partial_a g^{bc}p_bp_c,\quad C_m=0.$$

On the massive future branch $m>0$, these equations are equivalent to stationary paths of the mathematical square-root functional $S[x]=-mc\int_a^b\sqrt{-g(x\prime,x\prime)}\,d\lambda$ on future-timelike curves with fixed endpoints; the fibre-derivative covector is $p=mc\,x'^\flat/\sqrt{-g(x',x')}$, and proper-time gauge has $e=1/m$. For the separate nonzero future-null branch $m=0$, the equations describe a null geodesic with an arbitrary positive parameter multiplier; no proper-time parameter exists. In both cases the unparameterized path is a geodesic, and no existence or completeness claim is made.

Let $Q$ be a finite-dimensional smooth manifold as in [[def-rpm-h-cotangent-phase-space]], and write its cotangent phase space in induced coordinates $(q^i,p_i)$. With $\omega=dq^i\wedge dp_i$, define $X_H$ by $\iota_{X_H}\omega=dH$ and define the Poisson bracket by $\{F,G\}:=X_G(F)$. Then

$$X_H=\frac{\partial H}{\partial p_i}\frac{\partial}{\partial q^i}-\frac{\partial H}{\partial q^i}\frac{\partial}{\partial p_i},\qquad \{F,G\}=F_{q^i}G_{p_i}-F_{p_i}G_{q^i}.$$

The bracket is coordinate independent and makes smooth functions a Poisson algebra. If $H_t$ is smooth on an open time-dependent domain $D\subset\mathbb R\times T^*Q$, each solution of $\dot z=X_{H_t}(z)$ has local uniqueness and smooth dependence on initial data and parameters; on its actual interval,

$$\frac{d}{dt}F(t,z(t))=\partial_tF+\{F,H_t\}.$$

No completeness or global flow is asserted. If $H$ is smooth, each local time-$t$ flow map preserves ω.

Let $F:M^m\to N^n$ be smooth, let $q\in N$ be a regular value, and assume
$F^{-1}(q)$ is nonempty. Then $F^{-1}(q)$ is an embedded submanifold of
codimension $n$. Equivalently, it has dimension $m-n$.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold, let
$p\in M$, and let $n$ be an observer at $p$
([[def-gr-observer-and-rest-space]]). For $w\in T_pM$ write
$h=h_n$ and $\gamma(w):=-g_p(n,w)$.

1. If $w$ is nonzero future causal, then $\gamma(w)>0$.
2. If $w$ is future unit timelike, then $\gamma(w)\ge1$, with
   $\gamma(w)=1$ if and only if $w=n$, and
   $g_p(h(w),h(w))=\gamma(w)^2-1$.
3. If $w$ is unit timelike, then $w$ is future-directed if and only if
   $g_p(n,w)<0$, and past-directed if and only if $g_p(n,w)>0$; in particular
   $g_p(n,w)\neq0$ for such $w$.

derivations.claim: Use the supplied smooth tangent/cotangent structures under [A1] and the Lorentzian temporal-chart data [F1,F2]. Expand the metric matrix and invert its block form. Direct multiplication yields $g^{00}=-N^{-2}$, $g^{0i}=\beta^i/N^2$, $g^{ij}=h^{ij}-\beta^i\beta^j/N^2$. Therefore $$g^{ab}p_ap_b=-\frac{(p_0-\beta^ip_i)^2}{N^2}+h^{ij}p_ip_j.$$ The shell equation gives $p_0-\beta^ip_i=\pm N\kappa$. The future normal $n=N^{-1}(\partial_0-\beta^i\partial_i)$ has $p(n)=(p_0-\beta^ip_i)/N<0$ by [F6] for a nonzero future-causal shell covector, so the future branch is the negative root $p_0=\beta^ip_i-N\kappa$. Positive $h$ implies κ>0 except the excluded massless zero momentum.

The fibre derivative of $C_m$ with respect to $p_0$ is $g^{0b}p_b=\kappa/N>0$ on this branch. Thus the root is smooth and the shell is locally a graph over $(t,q^i,p_i)$; [F5] also gives the embedded regular-level structure.
On $x^0=ct$, the canonical term is $p_0c+p_i\dot q^i=p_i\dot q^i-H$. The constraint term vanishes on the solved shell, so the reduced action has the claimed integrand.

Applying the fixed-endpoint first-variation equations to the reduced canonical action gives $\dot q^i=\partial H/\partial p_i$, $\dot p_i=-\partial H/\partial q^i$; by [F4] these are Hamilton's equations for this time-dependent chart Hamiltonian. Smooth root and $N>0$ ensure the gauge parameter $t=x^0/c$ is valid on the stated interval; nothing here makes it global outside the chart.

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\sinh x:=\frac{\exp x-\exp(-x)}2,\qquad\cosh x:=\frac{\exp x+\exp(-x)}2,$$
$$\tanh x:=\frac{\sinh x}{\cosh x},\qquad\operatorname{sech}x:=\frac1{\cosh x}.$$
For $x\ne0$, define
$$\coth x:=\frac{\cosh x}{\sinh x},\qquad\operatorname{csch}x:=\frac1{\sinh x}.$$

The positivity of $\exp$ makes $\cosh x>0$ for every $x$. If $x\ne0$, then
$x\ne-x$, so strict increase of $\exp$ makes $\exp x\ne\exp(-x)$; hence
$\sinh x\ne0$. Thus all four quotients above are defined on exactly their
stated domains ([[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]],
[[thm-exponential-is-strictly-increasing]]).

For all real $x,y$,
$$\sinh(x+y)=\sinh x\cosh y+\cosh x\sinh y,\qquad\cosh(x+y)=\cosh x\cosh y+\sinh x\sinh y,$$
$$\cosh^2x-\sinh^2x=1,\qquad(\sinh x)'=\cosh x,\qquad(\cosh x)'=\sinh x.$$
Moreover $\sinh:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ is odd, strictly increasing, and onto;
$\cosh:\mathbb R\to[1,\infty)$ is even and positive, and its restriction
to $[0,\infty)$ is strictly increasing and onto $[1,\infty)$; and
$\tanh:\mathbb R\to(-1,1)$ is strictly increasing and onto. On their declared domains,
$$(\tanh x)'=\operatorname{sech}^2x,\quad(\coth x)'=-\operatorname{csch}^2x,\quad(\operatorname{sech}x)'=-\operatorname{sech}x\tanh x,\quad(\operatorname{csch}x)'=-\operatorname{csch}x\coth x.$$

The real exponential function is $C^\infty$, and for every $m\in\mathbb N$,
$$\exp^{(m)}=\exp.$$
In particular $(\exp)'=\exp$.

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) at which $g$ is differentiable
([[def-derivative]]), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be integrable
([[def-darboux-integral]]), let $F$ be its integral function
([[def-the-integral-function]]), and let $c \in [a,b]$ be a point at which $f$ is
continuous ([[def-continuity-real]]). Then $F$ is differentiable at $c$ as a
function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]) and

$$F'(c) \;=\; f(c) .$$

At $c = a$ and $c = b$ this is the one-sided statement, which is what
[[def-derivative]] means at those points: every point of a nondegenerate interval
is a limit point of it, so $F'(c)$ is a meaningful symbol at every $c \in [a,b]$,
and the difference quotient is taken over $[a,b] \setminus \{c\}$.

**Consequently, if $f$ is continuous on the whole of $[a,b]$, then $F$ is a
primitive of $f$ there**: $F' = f$ at every point of $[a,b]$.

**Continuity at $c$ is a hypothesis and it cannot be dropped.** For an integrable
$f$ that is discontinuous at $c$, $F'(c)$ may fail to exist, and it may exist and
differ from $f(c)$; both are exhibited on the companion page, by
an integrable function with no primitive and by a false
statement about the integral function.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$
([[def-continuity-real]]). Then $f$ is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]]) and Riemann
integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]).

**The proof gives more than integrability: it gives a partition that works.** For
every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the uniform partition into $N$ parts already
satisfies $U(f,P) - L(f,P) < \varepsilon$, as soon as $N$ is large enough that
$(b-a)/\iota(N)$ is below the $\delta$ that uniform continuity supplies for
$\varepsilon/\bigl(2(b-a)\bigr)$. Uniform continuity is exactly what makes one
$\delta$ serve all $N$ subintervals at once, and it is the only place where the
compactness of $[a,b]$ is used.

Restrict [[def-rpm-charge-spin-model]] to its flat affine Minkowski branch, with signature $(-,+,+,+)$, proper time $\tau$ in seconds, future four-velocity $U=dx/d\tau$ satisfying $\eta(U,U)=-c^2$, constant primitive $m>0$ in kilograms and nonzero charge $q\in\mathbb R$ in coulombs. Let the prescribed external electromagnetic two-form $F$ be $C^2$ on an open neighborhood of the worldline; use the component convention $F_{0i}=-E_i/c$, $F_{ij}=\epsilon_{ijk}B_k$ of [[def-em-electromagnetic-tensor]]. Let $a:=dU/d\tau$ and

$$\alpha:=q/m,\qquad \tau_e:=\frac{q^2}{6\pi\epsilon_0mc^3}>0,\qquad f_0^a:=\alpha F^a{}_bU^b,$$

where $\epsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$ follows [[def-em-si-conventions]]. Adopt the flat LAD effective equation

$$a^a=f_0^a+\tau_e\left(\frac{da^a}{d\tau}-\frac{\eta_{bc}a^ba^c}{c^2}U^a\right).$$

The derivative is the ordinary derivative in an inertial affine chart. Its dimensions are consistent: $a$ and $f_0$ are accelerations, the parenthesized term has acceleration per second, and $\tau_e$ is a time. This is an adopted effective model equation for sufficiently regular curves (at least $C^3$); it is not asserted to be an exact law of nature, a point-source Maxwell construction, or a globally well-posed dynamics. In particular, no existence, uniqueness, stability, or empirical claim is part of this postulate.

Use of the equation as a reduced physical approximation carries the source qualification that radiation reaction be small relative to the applied Lorentz force in the particle's instantaneous rest frame (the inertial frame momentarily comoving with $U$). This postulate neither asserts that condition for arbitrary $F$ nor supplies a numerical threshold; the qualification is not used to deduce the local ODE results or the force-free counterexample.

Let $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be an oriented, time-oriented affine Minkowski space of dimension four with signature $(-,+,+,+)$, and fix an inertial chart $(x^0,x^1,x^2,x^3)$ with $x^0=ct$, $c>0$. Let $O\subseteq A$ be open and let $F$ be a $C^2$ alternating covariant two-tensor on $O$. In this chart write $F^a{}_b:=\eta^{ac}F_{cb}$ and let $\partial_b$ denote the coordinate partial derivative. Fix constants $\alpha\in\mathbb R$ and $\tau_e\geq0$. For every $U\in V$, define

$$\Pi_U{}^a{}_b:=\delta^a_b+\frac{U^aU_b}{c^2},\qquad f_0^a(x,U):=\alpha F^a{}_b(x)U^b,$$

$$B^a(x,U):=\alpha(\partial_bF^a{}_c)(x)U^bU^c +\alpha^2F^a{}_b(x)F^b{}_c(x)U^c, \qquad a_{\rm LL}^a(x,U):=f_0^a(x,U)+\tau_e\Pi_U{}^a{}_bB^b(x,U).$$

For the physical interpretation, $x^a$ are in metres, $\tau$ is in seconds, $c$ is in metres per second, $U$ is in metres per second, $\alpha=q/m$, and $\tau_e$ is a time. Here a **proper-time parameter** means that the parameter is measured in seconds and the four-velocity is normalized by $\eta(U,U)=-c^2$; define the future unit shell by $\mathcal S^+:=\{U\in C^+:\eta(U,U)=-c^2\}$. For each initial datum $(x_0,U_0)\in O\times V$ with $U_0\in\mathcal S^+$, the system

$$\frac{dx^a}{d\tau}=U^a,\qquad \frac{dU^a}{d\tau}=a_{\rm LL}^a(x,U),\qquad (x(0),U(0))=(x_0,U_0)$$

has a unique local solution on an open proper-time interval about $0$. Along that interval $\eta(U,U)=-c^2$ and $U$ remains future directed. This is a local ODE statement: it makes no claim of global existence for arbitrary $F$.

derivations.claim: The integral defining $x$ is well-defined on every compact $\tau$ interval because $U$ is smooth by [F2]. The fundamental theorem [F2] gives $\dot x=U$. By [F1], $\eta(U,U)=c^2(-\cosh^2\theta+\sinh^2\theta)=-c^2$. Also $U^0=c\cosh\theta>0$, so $U$ is future directed in the chosen inertial chart. Thus $\tau$ is proper time and $x$ is future timelike.

Differentiating with [F1, F2] gives $$a=c\theta'(\sinh\theta,\cosh\theta,0,0),\qquad \dot a=c\theta''(\sinh\theta,\cosh\theta,0,0)+c(\theta')^2(\cosh\theta,\sinh\theta,0,0), \qquad \eta(a,a)=c^2(\theta')^2.$$ Consequently $\dot a-\eta(a,a)U/c^2=c\theta''(\sinh\theta,\cosh\theta,0,0)$, and the force-free equation [F3] is equivalent to $\theta'=\tau_e\theta''$. The chosen $\theta$ has $\theta'=Ae^{(\tau-\tau_0)/\tau_e}$ and $\theta''=\theta'/\tau_e$, so the equation holds identically. This proves that the curve solves the adopted LAD equation for every real proper time.

The invariant $\eta(a,a)=c^2(\theta')^2$ gives $\sqrt{\eta(a,a)}=c|A|e^{(\tau-\tau_0)/\tau_e}$, which is unbounded toward the future. For $F=0$, [F4] gives $a_{\rm LL}=0$, hence its local solutions have constant $U$. The displayed LAD solution is non-inertial since $A\ne0$, so it demonstrates that the force-free LAD equation admits runaway solutions even though the reduced LL force-free field does not. This is an ODE comparison, not an empirical conclusion.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be integrable
([[def-darboux-integral]]), let $F$ be its integral function
([[def-the-integral-function]]), and let $c \in [a,b]$ be a point at which $f$ is
continuous ([[def-continuity-real]]). Then $F$ is differentiable at $c$ as a
function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]) and

$$F'(c) \;=\; f(c) .$$

At $c = a$ and $c = b$ this is the one-sided statement, which is what
[[def-derivative]] means at those points: every point of a nondegenerate interval
is a limit point of it, so $F'(c)$ is a meaningful symbol at every $c \in [a,b]$,
and the difference quotient is taken over $[a,b] \setminus \{c\}$.

**Consequently, if $f$ is continuous on the whole of $[a,b]$, then $F$ is a
primitive of $f$ there**: $F' = f$ at every point of $[a,b]$.

**Continuity at $c$ is a hypothesis and it cannot be dropped.** For an integrable
$f$ that is discontinuous at $c$, $F'(c)$ may fail to exist, and it may exist and
differ from $f(c)$; both are exhibited on the companion page, by
an integrable function with no primitive and by a false
statement about the integral function.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$
([[def-continuity-real]]). Then $f$ is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]]) and Riemann
integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]).

**The proof gives more than integrability: it gives a partition that works.** For
every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the uniform partition into $N$ parts already
satisfies $U(f,P) - L(f,P) < \varepsilon$, as soon as $N$ is large enough that
$(b-a)/\iota(N)$ is below the $\delta$ that uniform continuity supplies for
$\varepsilon/\bigl(2(b-a)\bigr)$. Uniform continuity is exactly what makes one
$\delta$ serve all $N$ subintervals at once, and it is the only place where the
compactness of $[a,b]$ is used.

The real exponential function is $C^\infty$, and for every $m\in\mathbb N$,
$$\exp^{(m)}=\exp.$$
In particular $(\exp)'=\exp$.

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) at which $g$ is differentiable
([[def-derivative]]), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f, g : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be integrable
([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then:

1. **Nonnegativity.** If $f(x) \ge 0$ for every $x \in [a,b]$ then
   $\int_a^b f \ge 0$.
2. **Monotonicity.** If $f(x) \le g(x)$ for every $x \in [a,b]$ then
   $$\int_a^b f \;\le\; \int_a^b g .$$
3. **Two-sided bound.** If $m \le f(x) \le M$ for every $x \in [a,b]$, with
   $m, M$ real, then
   $$m\,(b-a) \;\le\; \int_a^b f \;\le\; M\,(b-a) .$$

**Equality in claim 1 does not force $f$ to vanish.** A nonnegative integrable
function with integral $0$ may be positive at infinitely many points; that is
[[fs-nonnegative-integrable-with-zero-integral-vanishes]] on the previous page's
companion. Under the additional hypothesis of continuity the conclusion does
hold, and that is [[thm-nonnegative-continuous-with-zero-integral-vanishes]]
below.

**Claim 2 is stated for $a < b$ and is not orientation-invariant.** With the
convention of [[def-oriented-integral]], $f \le g$ gives
$\int_u^v f \le \int_u^v g$ when $u \le v$ and the reverse inequality when
$u \ge v$, since both sides change sign together.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ satisfy

$$m \;\le\; f(x) \;\le\; M \qquad \text{for every } x \in [a,b],$$

with $m, M$ real. Then $f$ is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]]), so its Darboux sums
and integrals are defined ([[def-darboux-sums]], [[def-darboux-integral]]), and
for **every** partition $P$ of $[a,b]$ ([[def-partition-and-refinement]])

$$m(b-a) \;\le\; L(f,P) \;\le\; \underline{\int_a^b} f \;\le\; \overline{\int_a^b} f \;\le\; U(f,P) \;\le\; M(b-a) .$$

In particular, taking $f$ to be the constant function with value $c$:

$$\int_a^b c \;=\; c\,(b-a) ,$$

the constant function being integrable, with $L(f,P) = U(f,P) = c(b-a)$ for
every partition $P$.

For every real $x$, $\exp(x)>0$ and
$$\exp(-x)=\frac1{\exp(x)}.$$

Let $(X,d)$ be a nonempty compact metric space ([[def-metric-compactness]],
[[def-metric-space]]) and let $f : X \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous
([[def-metric-continuity]]), $\mathbb{R}$ carrying its usual metric
$d_{\mathbb{R}}(s,t) = |s-t|$ ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]). Then the
image $f[X]$ is bounded above and below ([[def-bounded-set]]), and it has a
maximum and a minimum ([[def-max-min]]): there are points
$x_{\max}, x_{\min} \in X$ with

$$f(x_{\min}) \;\le\; f(x) \;\le\; f(x_{\max}) \qquad \text{for every } x \in X,$$

and then $f(x_{\max}) = \sup f[X]$ and $f(x_{\min}) = \inf f[X]$
([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-infimum]]).

Nonemptiness of $X$ is a hypothesis and not an oversight: for $X = \emptyset$ the
image is empty and has neither a supremum nor a maximum. No choice principle is
used.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.
The exponential function is continuous and strictly increasing on $\mathbb R$.

$$\exp(x)\to+\infty\quad(x\to+\infty),\qquad \exp(x)\to0\quad(x\to-\infty),$$
and the range of $\exp$ is contained in $(0,\infty)$ and is unbounded above with infimum $0$.

derivations.claim: Define $I(t):=\int_t^\infty e^{(t-s)/\tau_e}F_{\rm ext}(s)\,ds$, interpreting the integral as a finite Riemann integral after any upper truncation beyond $\max\{t,T\}$; compact support makes the value independent of that truncation. For $t<T$, write $I(t)=e^{t/\tau_e}\int_t^T e^{-s/\tau_e}F_{\rm ext}(s)\,ds$. By [F1] the integrand is integrable on this compact interval, and [F2] together with the fundamental theorem gives $$I'(t)=-F_{\rm ext}(t)+\frac{1}{\tau_e}I(t)\qquad (t<T).$$ For $a=I/(m\tau_e)$ this identity becomes $\tau_e a'= -F_{\rm ext}/m+a$, which rearranges to the displayed Abraham–Lorentz equation. For $t>T$, both $I$ and $F_{\rm ext}$ vanish, so the same equation holds. At $t=T$, smoothness and support imply $F_{\rm ext}(T)=0$, and the one-sided derivatives agree with the displayed identity.

For $t\geq T$, the integration interval contains no point where $F_{\rm ext}$ is nonzero, so $a(t)=0$. For $t<0$, continuity and nonnegativity of the nonzero pulse give a closed subinterval of $(0,T)$ on which $F_{\rm ext}\geq d>0$. The exponential factor is positive and continuous there by [F2, F4]; its minimum is positive by [F5]. The integral over that subinterval is strictly positive by the lower bound [F3], and all remaining contributions are nonnegative. Thus $a(t)>0$. Since $a(t)=0$ for $t\geq T$, it satisfies the future boundary condition.

If $a_1,a_2$ are two solutions, their difference $d=a_1-a_2$ satisfies $d'=d/\tau_e$. The product rule gives $(e^{-t/\tau_e}d(t))'=0$, so [F6] implies this product is a constant $C$. By [F4], $d(t)=Ce^{t/\tau_e}$; if $C\ne0$, then [F7] makes $|d(t)|\to\infty$ as $t\to+\infty$, contradicting $d(t)\to0$. Hence $C=0$ and $d=0$, proving uniqueness. Together with step 2.1, the unique future-decaying solution is strictly positive for all $t<0$: this pre-acceleration is a property of the stated model equation, not an empirical claim.

Step 2.1 selects one positive subinterval from continuity for the fixed pulse and uses no choice axiom.
