citations.quote:
Let $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be an oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space
([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]), with orientation fixed as a positive ray of
the determinant line $\Lambda^4V$
([[def-determinant-line-orientation-of-a-finite-dimensional-real-vector-space]])
and with the corresponding class of positively oriented ordered bases of $V$
([[def-orientation-of-a-finite-dimensional-real-vector-space]]); by
[[prop-orientations-and-positive-basis-classes-agree-in-positive-dimension]] the
positive ray selects exactly one such class for $\dim V=4>0$.

An **inertial frame** of the model is a tuple $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ consisting
of an event $o\in A$ and an ordered basis $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of $V$ that is

1. **$\eta$-orthonormal**: $\eta(e_a,e_b)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$ for all $a,b$ ([[lem-lorentz-form-has-orthonormal-basis]]);
2. **future**: $e_0\in C^+$, i.e. $e_0$ is future timelike; and
3. **positively oriented**: the ordered basis lies in the positive-basis class
   selected by the fixed orientation.

The event $o$ is the **origin** of the frame and $e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3$ are its
**basis vectors**.

**Inertial charts.** For an inertial frame $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$, define

$$E:\mathbb R^4\longrightarrow V,\qquad E(u):=\sum_{a=0}^3u^ae_a .$$

Then $E$ is a linear isomorphism ([[def-linear-isomorphism-and-invertible-linear-map]]):
it is linear by construction, and it is bijective because
$(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ is an ordered basis, every $v\in V$ having exactly one
coordinate list $u$ with $v=\sum_au^ae_a$
([[thm-unique-coordinates-with-respect-to-an-ordered-basis]]). The **inertial
chart** of the frame is the map

$$x:A\longrightarrow\mathbb R^4,\qquad x(p):=E^{-1}(p-o),$$

and its values $x^a(p)$ are the **inertial coordinates of the event $p$** in the
frame. Since $E$ and $v\mapsto p+v$ are bijections, $x$ is a bijection
$A\to\mathbb R^4$; and $x(p)=0$ exactly when $p-o=0_V$, that is, exactly when
$p=o$.

**Transition law.** Let $(o';e'_0,e'_1,e'_2,e'_3)$ be another inertial frame
with chart $x'$, and let $M=(M^b_a)$ be the change-of-basis matrix defined by
$e'_a=\sum_bM^b_ae_b$, a $4\times4$ real matrix that is invertible because both
families are ordered bases. Then $E'(u)=\sum_au^ae'_a=E(Mu)$ for all
$u\in\mathbb R^4$, for the matrix-vector product $Mu$ in the coordinates of the
first frame, because $\sum_au^a\sum_bM^b_ae_b=\sum_b(\sum_aM^b_au^a)e_b$; hence
$E'=E\circ M$ and $E'^{-1}=M^{-1}\circ E^{-1}$, so for every event $p$,

$$x'(p)=M^{-1}\bigl(x(p)-x(o')\bigr)=M^{-1}x(p)-M^{-1}x(o') .$$

In particular the transition between two inertial charts is an affine map of
$\mathbb R^4$ with invertible linear part $M^{-1}$ and constant part
$-M^{-1}x(o')$, and it is a bijection of $\mathbb R^4$ with inverse
$u\mapsto Mu+x(o')$, which is the transition in the reverse direction.

**The inertial atlas.** The **inertial atlas** of the model is the family of
all inertial frames together with their inertial charts. Its charts are
available at every event by [[lem-future-oriented-inertial-frames-exist]], which
supplies for every $o\in A$ an inertial frame with origin $o$; and any two of
its charts are related by the affine transition displayed above.

This framework fixes the following SI coordinate and unit conventions for the
oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ and its inertial
charts ([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]],
[[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]).

1. **Adopted conversion constant.** The framework uses a positive constant $c$
   with unit metre per second, $\mathrm m/\mathrm s$, interpreted as the
   **speed of light in vacuum** under the framework's light postulate. In SI
   its numerical value is exactly $299\,792\,458$ by the definition of the
   metre (BIPM, *SI defining constants*, table row $c$). This exact unit
   convention does not prove that the ideal-light model describes nature;
   measurements and realizations of units still have uncertainty.
2. **Coordinates.** In every inertial chart $x=(x^0,x^1,x^2,x^3)$ define the
   coordinate-time map $t:A\to\mathbb R$ by $t(p)=x^0(p)/c$, with unit second
   $\mathrm s$, and assign unit metre $\mathrm m$ to every $x^a$. An **at-rest
   line of this frame** is $s\mapsto o+cs e_0+\sum_{i=1}^3r^ie_i$, $s\in\mathbb R$,
   for fixed spatial coordinates $(r^1,r^2,r^3)$ in metres; its coordinate
   time is $s$. Interpreting coordinate-time differences as readings of
   synchronized ideal clocks on these lines is a physical assumption stated
   in the clock postulate, not a consequence of assigning units.
3. **Metric components.** The matrix $\eta_{ab}=\eta(e_a,e_b)$ in the frame is
   $\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$ with **dimensionless** entries. Thus
   $I(p,q)=\eta(q-p,q-p)=-(\Delta x^0)^2+\sum_{i=1}^3(\Delta x^i)^2$
   carries unit $\mathrm m^2$.
4. **Proper time of a straight segment.** For a timelike displacement $q-p$,
   the affine straight segment is $s\mapsto p+s(q-p)$, $s\in[0,1]$. Define its
   positive **proper-time length** as

   $$\tau:=c^{-1}\sqrt{-\eta(q-p,q-p)}.$$

   It has unit second, since $c^{-1}$ converts the square-root interval in
   metres into seconds. This length is positive even if the segment is
   oriented toward the past; a physical advancing clock uses future orientation.
5. **Kinematic bookkeeping.** Let $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open interval
   with parameter $\tau$ in seconds, and let $\gamma:J\to A$ have $C^2$
   coordinates $y=x\circ\gamma:J\to\mathbb R^4$
   ([[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]). With
   $E(u)=\sum_au^ae_a$, require $U(\tau):=E(y'(\tau))\in C^+$ and
   $\eta(U,U)=-c^2$. This is the **proper-time normalization** used here for
   units; the general construction of a proper-time parameter is developed
   later. The **four-velocity** is $U:J\to V$, with components $U^a=(y^a)'$
   and unit $\mathrm m/\mathrm s$. The **four-acceleration** is
   $\mathcal A=E(y''):J\to V$, with unit $\mathrm m/\mathrm s^2$.
   For a positive constant mass parameter $m$ in kilograms, define
   **four-momentum** $P=mU:J\to V$, with unit
   $\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm m/\mathrm s$, and **energy measured by this frame**
   $\mathcal E=cP^0=-c\eta(e_0,P):J\to\mathbb R$, with unit joule
   $\mathrm J=\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm m^2/\mathrm s^2$. The equality follows from
   $\eta(e_0,P)=-P^0$. These are definitions for dimensional bookkeeping;
   the physical particle interpretation and dynamics belong to later pages.
6. **Temporal-coordinate convention.** Replacing $x^0$ by $t=x^0/c$ pulls
   the interval expression back to $-c^2(\Delta t)^2+\sum_i(\Delta x^i)^2$.
   Thus $g_{tt}=-c^2$ has unit $\mathrm m^2/\mathrm s^2$, the spatial
   components remain dimensionless, and mixed time-space components have unit
   $\mathrm m/\mathrm s$ (and equal zero in this inertial chart). Formulas
   must be transformed when changing this convention.
7. **Natural units.** A presentation with $c=1$ identifies temporal and spatial
   units by this conversion factor; it requires an explicit restoration table
   for $c$. It does not assert that the SI numerical value of $c$ is $1$.

**Status.** These are conventions and dimensional bookkeeping for the model.
The SI numerical value of $c$ is exact by unit definition; the physical
interpretation and applicability of the model remain adopted and empirically
testable. SI unit status does not make a quantity primitive in the theory.

Adopt [[post-sr-inertial-covariance]], [[post-sr-ideal-clocks-and-light]] and [[post-sr-causal-signal-propagation]], and the SI conventions of [[def-sr-si-units-and-coordinate-conventions]] ($x^0 = c t$). Let $x = (x^0,x^1,x^2,x^3)$ be the chart of an inertial frame ([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]) and let $W := \{x^1 > |x^0|\}$ be the right wedge. Let $\Phi$ and $n$ be the Rindler chart and congruence of [[thm-sr-fermi-walker-and-rigid-observer-examples]] (b): $\Phi(\theta,\rho,y,z) = (\rho \sinh \theta, \rho \cosh \theta, y, z)$ on $\mathbb R \times (0,\infty) \times \mathbb R^2$ with inverse $\rho = \sqrt{(x^1)^2 - (x^0)^2}$, $\theta = \frac12 \log((x^1+x^0)/(x^1-x^0))$, pullback metric $-\rho^2 d\theta^2 + d\rho^2 + dy^2 + dz^2$, and acceleration field $a_{\mathrm{cg}} = \nabla_n n = \rho^{-1} \partial_\rho$. Fix $\rho_0 > 0$ and real $y_0,z_0$, and let $O$ be the congruence worldline $\rho = \rho_0$, $y = y_0$, $z = z_0$, parametrized by its proper time $\tau$ with $\theta = c \tau/\rho_0$; by [[def-sr-proper-acceleration]] its proper acceleration is $c^2/\rho_0$. Write $U(q) := q^0 + q^1$ and $V(q) := q^0 - q^1$ for events $q$, so that $U = \rho e^{\theta}$ and $V = -\rho e^{-\theta}$ on $W$, and write $\le$ and $J^+$, $J^-$ for the causal reachability relations of [[def-sr-causal-reachability-in-affine-minkowski-space]]. Then, conditionally on the adopted model:

(i) **Chart domain and light rays.** $\Phi$ is a smooth bijection of $\mathbb R \times (0,\infty) \times \mathbb R^2$ onto $W$ with the stated smooth inverse, so the chart domain is exactly $W$ and $\rho = 0$ is not part of its coordinate domain. The boundary of $W$ in the affine model is $\{x^1 = |x^0|\}$, with arbitrary $x^2,x^3$: it is the union of the two null half-planes $\{x^1 = x^0 \ge 0\}$ and $\{x^1 = -x^0 \ge 0\}$. These half-planes are portions of the full null planes appearing as causal horizons in (ii); the full planes are not the wedge boundary. Along the worldline $\rho = \rho_0$ one has $V = -\rho_0 e^{-\theta} \to 0^-$ and $U \to +\infty$ as $\theta \to +\infty$, while $U = \rho_0 e^{\theta} \to 0^+$ and $V \to -\infty$ as $\theta \to -\infty$. The future null straight lines of the model that lie in the plane $y = y_0$, $z = z_0$ and meet $O$ are exactly the lines of constant $V$ (on which $d\theta = +d\rho/\rho$) and the lines of constant $U$ (on which $d\theta = -d\rho/\rho$).

(ii) **Causal horizons.** An event $q$ satisfies $q \le p$ for some event $p$ of $O$ if and only if $V(q) < 0$; an event $q$ satisfies $p \le q$ for some event $p$ of $O$ if and only if $U(q) > 0$. Consequently no event with $V(q) \ge 0$ can ever influence $O$; this set contains the null plane $\{x^1 = x^0\}$, the left wedge $\{x^1 < -|x^0|\}$ and the future wedge $\{x^0 > |x^1|\}$; and no event with $U(q) \le 0$ can ever be influenced by $O$, a set containing the null plane $\{x^1 = -x^0\}$, the left wedge and the past wedge $\{x^0 < -|x^1|\}$. The null plane $\{x^1 = x^0\}$ is the boundary of the causal past of $O$ (the future horizon: the surface its worldline approaches as $\theta \to +\infty$), and the null plane $\{x^1 = -x^0\}$ is the boundary of the causal future of $O$ (the past horizon); every event of the left wedge is causally unrelated to $O$ in both directions. The same criteria with $O$ any other congruence worldline $\rho = \rho_1$, $y = y_1$, $z = z_1$ hold verbatim: the constants $\rho_0$, $y_0$, $z_0$ do not enter.

(iii) **Radar time and distance to a coaxial congruence reflector.** Fix $\rho_m > 0$ with $\rho_m \ne \rho_0$ and let $R_m$ be the congruence worldline $\rho = \rho_m$, $y = y_0$, $z = z_0$ (a second uniformly accelerated observer, coaxial with $O$, with proper acceleration $c^2/\rho_m$). Let $e_-$ be the event of $O$ at parameter $\theta_e$ (so $\tau(e_-) = \rho_0 \theta_e/c$ up to the base point of $\tau$), let $q_m$ be the event of $R_m$ lying on the future null straight line from $e_-$ in the plane $y = y_0$, $z = z_0$, and let $e_+$ be the event of $O$ lying on the future null straight line from $q_m$; the reflection at $q_m$ is idealized as instantaneous and as leaving $R_m$'s motion unchanged, as in [[def-sr-operational-radar-protocol]]. Then $e_-, q_m, e_+$ exist uniquely, the Rindler time of $q_m$ is $\theta_m = \theta_e + |\log(\rho_m/\rho_0)|$, the return event satisfies $\theta(e_+) = \theta_e + 2|\log(\rho_m/\rho_0)|$ and $(\theta_e + \theta(e_+))/2 = \theta_m$, so the round trip lasts $2|\log(\rho_m/\rho_0)|$ in Rindler time and $(2\rho_0/c)|\log(\rho_m/\rho_0)|$ in $O$'s proper time. The radar protocol therefore assigns to $q_m$ the radar time $\tau_{\mathrm{rad}}(q_m) = (\rho_0/c) \theta_m$ plus the base constant of $\tau$ and the radar distance $\rho_{\mathrm{rad}}(q_m) = \rho_0 |\log(\rho_m/\rho_0)|$; within this coaxial family the radar-time level sets are the intersections of the Rindler rest slices $\theta=\mathrm{const}$ with $y=y_0$, $z=z_0$, excluding the observer radius $\rho_0$ ([[def-sr-simultaneity-slice-and-rest-distance]]). The radar distance is not the rest distance: in the slice $\theta = \theta_m$ the two worldlines are at rest distance $|\rho_m - \rho_0|$, whereas for $\rho_m = 2\rho_0$ the radar distance is $\rho_0 \log 2 < \rho_0$, because $\log$ is strictly increasing and $e > 2$ implies $\log 2 < \log e = 1$ ([[cor-two-less-than-e-less-than-three]], [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]]). For every distinct positive reflector radius the notions differ: with $r = \rho_m/\rho_0$, one has $\log r < r - 1$ when $r > 1$ and $-\log r > 1 - r$ when $0 < r < 1$. The two distance formulas agree only at $r = 1$, where both have the continuous degenerate value zero. The coincident case is not a nonzero emission-reflection-reception triple of the protocol, whose distinct-reflector hypothesis remains in force. As $\rho_m \to 0^+$ the round-trip proper time and the radar distance grow without bound while the reflector's proper acceleration $c^2/\rho_m$ diverges; as $\rho_m \to +\infty$ the round-trip proper time and the radar distance also grow without bound while the reflector's proper acceleration tends to $0$.

(iv) **Restrictions of the protocol.** No event with $V \ge 0$ --- in particular no event of the horizon plane $\{x^1 = x^0\}$, of the left wedge or of the future wedge --- can be assigned a radar time or radar distance by this protocol from $O$, because by (ii) it cannot causally precede any reception event on $O$: the required reflection-to-reception leg is impossible. Separately, every event with $U \le 0$ lacks an emission-to-reflection leg from $O$. Thus any event admitting this radar triple must satisfy $U > 0$ and $V < 0$, equivalently it must belong to $W$; the horizon is at infinite radar distance in the limit $\rho_m \to 0^+$. For example $q = x^{-1}(2\rho_0,0,y_0,z_0)$ has $U(q) = V(q) = 2\rho_0 > 0$. It is causally after $O$ at $\theta = 0$, since the displacement is $(2\rho_0,-\rho_0,0,0)$, future timelike, and it even lies on a future null ray from $O$ at $\theta = \log 2$, with displacement $(5\rho_0/4,-5\rho_0/4,0,0)$. Nevertheless it cannot send a causal return to $O$, so it receives no radar assignment from $O$. The protocol therefore does not extend to a global coordinate system of $A$.

(v) **Scope.** All clauses are conditional computations and readings in flat classical spacetime with ideal clocks, ideal light rays and ideal reflectors, for the specified congruence worldlines. They are not empirical claims and contain no measurement, apparatus, source, detector or statistical content; gravitation, media, dispersion, finite resolution, quantum effects and material models of the reflector are excluded. No choice principle is used.

Adopt as physical assumptions of the special-relativity framework the following
two statements, with the SI coordinate and unit conventions of
[[def-sr-si-units-and-coordinate-conventions]].

**(i) Ideal clocks.** Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nondegenerate interval and
$\gamma:I\to A$ a curve. Choose an inertial chart $\chi$ with
$E(u)=\sum_au^ae_a$ as in [[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]. Require
$y:=\chi\circ\gamma:I\to\mathbb R^4$ to be $C^1$ on the interior of $I$,
with its derivative extending continuously to any included endpoints, where
it is the one-sided derivative. Define the displacement-valued derivative by
$\dot\gamma(s):=E(y'(s))\in V$ and require $\dot\gamma(s)\in C^+$ everywhere,
including such endpoints. This derivative is chart-independent: a second
chart has coordinates $\widetilde y=M^{-1}(y-\chi(o'))$, so its
parameter derivative is $M^{-1}\mathrm dy/\mathrm ds$, while its basis map
is $E'=EM$; their product is $E\,\mathrm dy/\mathrm ds$.

An **ideal clock on this curve** has a reading map $\sigma:I\to\mathbb R$
in seconds, specified up to an additive constant, with, for all $a<b$ in $I$,

$$\sigma(b)-\sigma(a)=c^{-1}\int_a^b\sqrt{-\eta\bigl(\dot\gamma(s),\dot\gamma(s)\bigr)}\,\mathrm ds .$$

The integrand is positive and continuous on $[a,b]$: the coordinate derivatives
are continuous, $\eta$ is a finite bilinear expression, and the square root
is continuous at every positive argument, as follows from
$|\sqrt r-\sqrt q|=|r-q|/(\sqrt r+\sqrt q)$ for $r,q>0$.
Thus [[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]] applies to this compact interval
and gives a well-defined Riemann integral. The reading rule contains no
additional acceleration-dependent correction (**clock hypothesis**); it does
not require $C^2$ regularity or an acceleration to exist. This is an adopted
physical interpretation of the length integral, not a proof about real clocks.

**(ii) Ideal light.** In vacuum, the **ideal light rays** are the oriented
straight lines parametrized by $\ell:\mathbb R\to A$,
$\ell(\lambda)=p+\lambda v$, where $p\in A$ and $v\in V$ is future null;
increasing $\lambda$ specifies their future direction. In an inertial chart
$\chi$ their coordinate map is

$$\chi(\ell(\lambda))=\chi(p)+\lambda\,(v^0,v^1,v^2,v^3).$$

Since the chart's time-axis vector is future, the cone description of
[[lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components]] gives
$v^0=\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert>0$. With $t=\chi^0/c$ the spatial
coordinate velocity is $c(v^1,v^2,v^3)/v^0$ and has Euclidean magnitude $c$
in every inertial chart. The conversion constant is the same across charts;
its exact SI numerical value is a unit convention as specified in
[[def-sr-si-units-and-coordinate-conventions]], while the ideal-vacuum-light
interpretation is an adopted, empirically testable model assumption.

Let $c > 0$ and let $(A,V,\eta,C^{+})$ be an oriented time-oriented affine
Minkowski space ([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]).

**(a) Norm of the four-velocity.** Let $x : I \to A$ be a $C^{1}$ future
timelike worldline with four-velocity $U$
([[def-sr-four-velocity-and-four-acceleration]]). Then
$\eta(U(s),U(s)) = -c^{2}$ for every $s \in I$; equivalently the dimensionless
four-velocity $u = U/c$ satisfies $\eta(u,u) = -1$, and $U(s)$ is future
timelike. Thus the dimensionless four-velocity lies on the future unit
hyperboloid $\{v \in C^{+}:\eta(v,v)=-1\}$.

**(b) Orthogonality of the four-acceleration.** If $x$ is $C^{2}$ at $s$, then
$\eta(U(s),A(s)) = 0$: the four-acceleration has no component along the
four-velocity; if in addition $A(s) \ne 0$, then $A(s)$ is spacelike.

**(c) Rest space and projection.** Let $n \in V$ be future unit timelike,
$\eta(n,n) = -1$, and put $n^{\perp} := \{\,v \in V : \eta(n,v) = 0\,\}$
([[def-lorentz-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]]). Then $n^{\perp}$ is a
3-dimensional linear subspace of $V$, the restriction of $\eta$ to $n^{\perp}$
is positive definite, and the map $h : V \to V$, $h(v) := v + \eta(n,v)\,n$, is
linear, idempotent with $h \circ h = h$, has image $n^{\perp}$ and kernel
$\operatorname{span}(n)$, satisfies $h(n) = 0$ and $\eta(n,h(v)) = 0$ for all
$v \in V$, and every $v \in V$ has the unique decomposition
$v = -\eta(n,v)\,n + h(v)$. Moreover $|w| := \sqrt{\eta(w,w)}$ defines a norm
on $n^{\perp}$.

**(d) Relative velocity and Lorentz factor.** Let $n$ and $u$ be future unit
timelike vectors, put $\gamma := -\eta(n,u)$ and $w := c\,h(u)/\gamma$. Then
$\gamma \ge 1$, $w$ lies in $n^{\perp}$,
$u = \gamma\,(n + w/c)$, $|w|^{2} = c^{2}(1-\gamma^{-2}) < c^{2}$,
$\gamma = (1-|w|^{2}/c^{2})^{-1/2}$, and $\gamma = 1$ if and only if $u = n$.
The vector $w$ is the velocity of a worldline with four-velocity $cu$ relative
to the observer $n$, and $\gamma$ is its Lorentz factor.

**(e) Coordinate form.** Let $(o;e_0,\dots,e_3)$ be an inertial frame and let
$y$ be a $C^{1}$ future timelike worldline whose inertial coordinates are
$t \mapsto (ct,r(t))$, with coordinate velocity $w(t) := r'(t)$ in
$\mathbb{R}^{3}$ and, when $y$ is $C^{2}$, coordinate acceleration
$a(t) := w'(t)$. Then $|w(t)| < c$, the four-velocity is
$U = \gamma_w\,(c,w)$ with $\gamma_w := (1-|w|^{2}/c^{2})^{-1/2}$, and the
four-acceleration is $A = \gamma_w\,\frac{d}{dt}\bigl(\gamma_w(c,w)\bigr)$, so
that

$$A^{0} = \gamma_w^{4}\,\frac{w \cdot a}{c}, \qquad A_{\mathrm{vec}} = \gamma_w^{2}\,a + \gamma_w^{4}\,\frac{(w \cdot a)\,w}{c^{2}} ;$$

consequently
$\eta(A,A) = \gamma_w^{4}|a|^{2} + \gamma_w^{6}(w \cdot a)^{2}/c^{2} \ge 0$,
with $\eta(A,A) = 0$ if and only if $a = 0$, and $\eta(U,A) = 0$. For the
observer $n = e_0$ of the chart, clauses (c) and (d) specialize to
$\gamma = \gamma_w$ and $w_{\mathrm{rel}} = (0,w)$ in the frame coordinates, identified with $w$ via the spatial basis.

**(f) Scope.** The statement is a theorem about the affine Minkowski model with
a fixed positive constant $c$; it asserts no clock reading and identifies no
physical four-velocity. No choice principle is used.

Let $c>0$ and let $x:I\to A$ be a $C^2$ future timelike worldline in the affine Minkowski model ([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]], [[def-sr-regular-causal-curve-and-worldline]]), with generic parameter $s\in I$. Write $\tau:I\to\tau[I]$ for its proper-time function and $U(s):=x'(s)/\tau'(s)$, $A(s):=U'(s)/\tau'(s)$ for its four-velocity and four-acceleration ([[def-sr-four-velocity-and-four-acceleration]]). These are proper-time derivatives evaluated at the event $x(s)$; $s$ need not itself be proper time. Pointwise $\eta(U,U)=-c^2$, $\eta(U,A)=0$, and $A(s)$ is spacelike whenever it is nonzero ([[thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition]] (a),(b)).

**(a) Definition.** The **proper acceleration** of $x$ at the parameter value $s$ is the real number

$$a(s) := \sqrt{\eta(A(s),A(s))},$$

the nonnegative square root of [[def-rational-power]]. This is well defined for every $s \in I$. Indeed, fix an inertial chart of $A$ ([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]); since $x$ is $C^2$, the component functions of $A$ are continuous, and $\eta(A,A)$ is a sum of products of continuous component functions, hence continuous, by [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]]. If $A(s) = 0$ then $\eta(A,A) = 0$ at $s$, and if $A(s) \neq 0$ then $A(s)$ is spacelike and $\eta(A,A) > 0$ ([[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]]); in both cases the argument of the square root is nonnegative, so $a(s)$ is a well-defined nonnegative real number for every $s \in I$. With the SI coordinate and unit conventions of [[def-sr-si-units-and-coordinate-conventions]], in which $x^0 = c t$ with $t$ in seconds and the spatial coordinates are in metres while $\eta$ has the dimensionless matrix $\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$ in an inertial chart, the components of $A$ carry the unit metre per second squared and $\eta(A,A)$ carries the unit $(\text{metre per second squared})^2$, so $a$ carries the unit metre per second squared. The worldline is **uniformly accelerated** when $a$ is constant on $I$.

**(b) Agreement with the acceleration of a congruence.** Let $\Omega$ be a nonempty open subset of $A$ and let $n : \Omega \to V$ be an observer congruence with acceleration field $a_{\mathrm{cg}} := \nabla_n n$, where $\nabla$ is the flat covariant derivative of [[def-flat-covariant-derivative-on-affine-minkowski-space]] ([[def-sr-observer-congruence-and-kinematics]] (b)). If $x$ is a flow line of $n$ and $U = c n$ along $x$, then $A = c^2 a_{\mathrm{cg}}$ along $x$: the derivative along the worldline of the field $n$ is the covariant derivative $\nabla_{dx/d\tau} n = \nabla_{cn} n = c \nabla_n n = c\, a_{\mathrm{cg}}$, by the defining properties of the flat covariant derivative along curves ([[def-flat-covariant-derivative-on-affine-minkowski-space]] (d)), so $A = d(c n)/d\tau = c\, \nabla_{dx/d\tau} n = c^2 a_{\mathrm{cg}}$. Consequently $a = c^2 \sqrt{\eta(a_{\mathrm{cg}},a_{\mathrm{cg}})}$ along $x$: the proper acceleration is $c^2$ times the magnitude of the congruence acceleration. In particular the proper acceleration of a congruence worldline is determined by the congruence field alone, and such a worldline is uniformly accelerated exactly when $\eta(a_{\mathrm{cg}},a_{\mathrm{cg}})$ is constant along it.

**(c) Reading and scope.** This item defines a quantity of the model and fixes its name, its unit and its physical reading. The model reads $a(s)$ as the magnitude that an ideal accelerometer carried along the worldline would register at $s$; this ideal-instrument identification is adopted with the model in the same sense as the framework's ideal-clock reading of proper time and is not derived here. No accelerometer response law, calibration, frequency dependence, force law or interaction is specified or asserted; the definition asserts nothing about which bodies follow which worldlines; no measurement outcome and no statistical, uncertainty or empirical claim is made. No choice principle is used.

Adopt the SI coordinate and unit conventions of [[def-sr-si-units-and-coordinate-conventions]]: in every inertial chart $x^0=ct$ with $c>0$ in metres per second and spatial coordinates in metres, so $c$ is the model's conversion constant. Let $k$ be a future null wave covector and $\theta$ its affine phase ([[def-sr-affine-phase-and-wave-covector]]). Take $\theta$ dimensionless; its covector components then have unit $\mathrm m^{-1}$.

**Angular convention.** Here angles use radian arc length on the unit circle. An explicit construction, also fixing $\pi$, is $a(t):=2\int_0^t(1+r^2)^{-1}\,\mathrm dr$ for $0\le t\le1$, and $\pi:=2a(1)$. These are finite Riemann integrals ([[def-oriented-integral]]): the integrand is continuous with positive denominator by [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]] and integrable by [[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]]. By [[thm-ftc-first-part]], $a'(t)=2/(1+t^2)>0$; [[cor-mean-value-theorem]] makes $a$ strictly increasing, and [[thm-intermediate-value]] makes it a bijection onto $[0,\pi/2]$. This is the arc-length parameter of the quarter-circle $q(t)=((1-t^2)/(1+t^2),2t/(1+t^2))$: the sum, product and quotient rules of [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]] give $q'(t)=(-4t,2(1-t^2))/(1+t^2)^2$, hence $|q'(t)|=2/(1+t^2)$, and $|q(t)|=1$.

For $\alpha\in[0,\pi/2]$, let $t$ be the unique value with $a(t)=\alpha$ and define $\cos\alpha:=(1-t^2)/(1+t^2)$ and $\sin\alpha:=2t/(1+t^2)$; for $\alpha\in[\pi/2,\pi]$ use the unique $t$ with $a(t)=\pi-\alpha$ and define $\cos\alpha:=-(1-t^2)/(1+t^2)$ and $\sin\alpha:=2t/(1+t^2)$. The definitions agree at $\pi/2$. The rational function $(1-t^2)/(1+t^2)$ decreases continuously from $1$ to $0$, since its difference at $v>u\ge0$ is $-2(v^2-u^2)/[(1+v^2)(1+u^2)]<0$. Thus cosine is a strictly decreasing bijection $[0,\pi]\to[-1,1]$; write $\arccos$ for its inverse. For spatial coordinate vectors $v,w\in\mathbb R^3$ in one named inertial frame, write $v\cdot w:=\sum_{i=1}^3v_iw_i$ and $|v|:=\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^3v_i^2}$. If $v,w$ are nonzero, their norms are positive and their **angle** is $\arccos((v\cdot w)/(|v||w|))$: [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-finite]], applied to the three real coordinate entries, gives $|v\cdot w|\le|v||w|$, so division by $|v||w|>0$ puts the argument in $[-1,1]$. For unit vectors it is $\arccos(v\cdot w)$. These formulas give $\sin\alpha\ge0$ and $\sin^2\alpha+\cos^2\alpha=1$ on $[0,\pi]$ and fix a full turn as $2\pi$.

**(a) Frame data as wave data.** In the inertial chart of a frame $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ ([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]) let $(\varpi,s)$ be the frame data of $k$ given by [[lem-sr-null-covector-frame-data]], so $\varpi=-k(e_0)>0$ and $|s|=1$. Define the **angular frequency** $\omega:=c\varpi$ (unit $\mathrm s^{-1}$), the **linear frequency** $\nu:=\omega/(2\pi)$ (unit $\mathrm s^{-1}$, hertz), the **wave vector** $\kappa:=(\omega/c)s$ (unit $\mathrm m^{-1}$, with $|\kappa|=\omega/c$), the **wavelength** $\lambda:=2\pi/|\kappa|=2\pi c/\omega=c/\nu$ (unit $\mathrm m$), and the **propagation direction** $s$ (dimensionless). In these conventions the phase is $\theta(p)=-\omega t+\kappa\cdot x_{\mathrm{vec}}(p)+\mathrm{const}$ with $t:=x^0(p)/c$ the coordinate time in seconds, so the components of $k$ in the chart are

$$k_a=\bigl(-\omega/c,(\omega/c)s_1,(\omega/c)s_2,(\omega/c)s_3\bigr).$$

**(b) Observer frequency.** For an ideal observer whose four-velocity is $U_o=cn$ with $n\in V$ future unit timelike, $\eta(n,n)=-1$ ([[def-sr-four-velocity-and-four-acceleration]], [[thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition]]), define the **observer angular frequency** of the wave as

$$\omega_n:=-ck(n)=-k(U_o)\qquad(\text{unit }\mathrm s^{-1}),$$

and the **observer linear frequency** as $\omega_n/(2\pi)$. By [[lem-sr-phase-rate-along-worldline]] this is minus the rate of change of the phase with respect to the observer's own proper time, and the sign convention makes it positive.

**(c) Well-definedness.** $\varpi=-k(e_0)>0$ and $|s|=1$ in every inertial frame, hence $\omega>0$ and $\lambda>0$ are well defined and independent of the choices made in their computation (frame-data lemma); $\omega_n>0$ for every future unit timelike $n$ and every future null wave covector $k$ ([[lem-sr-future-causal-pairing-negative]], [[lem-sr-metric-duality-on-lorentz-vector-space]]), so every ideal observer reads a positive angular frequency, and $\omega_n$ depends only on $k$ and the observer vector $n$. The classification of $k$ as future null is the one of [[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]] and [[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]].

**(d) Scope.** This item fixes definitions, units and sign conventions only. It does not assert that any physical light is described by such a phase; that identification is adopted in post-sr-ideal-plane-wave-model. It contains no quantum identification of energy with $\hbar\omega$, no amplitude or intensity content, no medium or dispersion model, no source or detector model, and no measurement or empirical claim. No choice principle is used.

Adopt as physical assumptions of this framework, extending [[post-sr-ideal-clocks-and-light]] (ideal vacuum light rays are exactly the future null straight lines, with coordinate speed $c$ in every inertial chart) and [[post-sr-inertial-covariance]] (the affine Minkowski model, with the model's equations covariant under proper orthochronous affine Lorentz maps):

**(i) Ideal plane wave.** An ideal monochromatic light wave in vacuum is modeled, in any inertial chart, by a dimensionless affine phase $\theta$ with future null wave covector $k$ ([[def-sr-affine-phase-and-wave-covector]], [[lem-sr-null-covector-frame-data]]): the level sets of $\theta$ are the wave fronts, and the complete ray trajectories of this wave are the constant-phase lines $\lambda\mapsto p+\lambda k^\sharp$ for $\lambda\in\mathbb R$, whose tangents are future null. Their future portions from $p$ have images $p+\mathbb R_{\ge0}k^\sharp$. The complete trajectories are ideal light rays in the sense of [[post-sr-ideal-clocks-and-light]]; the portions are half-lines. The model is one ideal plane wave: constant wave covector, no medium, no dispersion, no absorption, no modulation or envelope, no boundary or source model, no intensity or polarization model.

**(ii) Frequency reading.** An ideal observer of the model with four-velocity $U_o=cn$ ($n$ future unit timelike) that receives this wave reads the angular frequency $\omega_n:=-ck(n)=-k(U_o)$ and the linear frequency $\omega_n/(2\pi)$ of [[def-sr-null-wave-covector-and-observer-frequency]], that is, minus the rate of change of the phase with respect to the observer's own proper time with the sign convention that this number is positive ([[lem-sr-phase-rate-along-worldline]], [[lem-sr-future-causal-pairing-negative]]). The reading is attached to the observer's worldline at the event of reception.

**(iii) Frequency comparisons.** Comparing the frequency of one wave between two ideal observers or between two inertial descriptions means comparing $\omega_n$ at specified reception events, or the frame data $(\omega,s)$ of the same phase function in specified inertial charts; this postulate asserts no Doppler or aberration formula, and comparing events requires propagating the phase along the specified observer worldlines.

**(iv) Scope and exclusions.** These are adopted idealizations, not deductions from experiment and not claims about nature. No quantum photon model and no identification of energy with $\hbar\omega$ is made; no claim is made that real light, real clocks, real receivers or real sources are exactly described; dispersive, absorbing, nonlinear or modulated media, finite line width, intensity, polarization, source and detector physics, gravitation, quantum effects and accelerated-observer reception are outside the model. Empirical tests of the model belong to the framework's experimental work and are not asserted here.

No choice principle is used in this formulation; the postulate is an adopted assumption of the model, not a proved assertion.

For all real $x,y$,
$$\sinh(x+y)=\sinh x\cosh y+\cosh x\sinh y,\qquad\cosh(x+y)=\cosh x\cosh y+\sinh x\sinh y,$$
$$\cosh^2x-\sinh^2x=1,\qquad(\sinh x)'=\cosh x,\qquad(\cosh x)'=\sinh x.$$
Moreover $\sinh:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ is odd, strictly increasing, and onto;
$\cosh:\mathbb R\to[1,\infty)$ is even and positive, and its restriction
to $[0,\infty)$ is strictly increasing and onto $[1,\infty)$; and
$\tanh:\mathbb R\to(-1,1)$ is strictly increasing and onto. On their declared domains,
$$(\tanh x)'=\operatorname{sech}^2x,\quad(\coth x)'=-\operatorname{csch}^2x,\quad(\operatorname{sech}x)'=-\operatorname{sech}x\tanh x,\quad(\operatorname{csch}x)'=-\operatorname{csch}x\coth x.$$

For $x>0$, $\log$ is differentiable and
$$\log'(x)=\frac1x,\qquad \log x=\int_1^x\frac{dt}{t}.$$

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\sinh x:=\frac{\exp x-\exp(-x)}2,\qquad\cosh x:=\frac{\exp x+\exp(-x)}2,$$
$$\tanh x:=\frac{\sinh x}{\cosh x},\qquad\operatorname{sech}x:=\frac1{\cosh x}.$$
For $x\ne0$, define
$$\coth x:=\frac{\cosh x}{\sinh x},\qquad\operatorname{csch}x:=\frac1{\sinh x}.$$

The positivity of $\exp$ makes $\cosh x>0$ for every $x$. If $x\ne0$, then
$x\ne-x$, so strict increase of $\exp$ makes $\exp x\ne\exp(-x)$; hence
$\sinh x\ne0$. Thus all four quotients above are defined on exactly their
stated domains ([[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]],
[[thm-exponential-is-strictly-increasing]]).

In the flat affine Minkowski model with signature $(-,+,+,+)$ and $x^0=ct$, use the smooth right-wedge chart and stationary congruence of [[pthm-sr-rindler-horizons-and-radar]]. A stationary observer has fixed $\rho>0,y,z$, worldline $z(\tau)$ on an open proper-time interval in seconds, and four-velocity $U=dz/d\tau$ with $\eta(U,U)=-c^2$. These are accelerated timelike worldlines, not global inertial frames.

Let $\theta$ be the dimensionless affine phase with constant nonzero future null covector $k=d\theta$ and ideal vacuum rays of [[post-sr-ideal-plane-wave-model]] (i). As an **additional local reception assumption**, adopt that an ideal point receiver comoving with a stationary Rindler observer assigns, at the event $z(\tau)$, the instantaneous received angular frequency

$$\omega(\tau):=-\frac{d(\theta\circ z)}{d\tau}=-k(U(\tau))>0,$$

and linear frequency $\nu(\tau)=\omega(\tau)/(2\pi)$ in the conventions of [[def-sr-null-wave-covector-and-observer-frequency]] and [[def-sr-si-units-and-coordinate-conventions]]. The phase derivative and positivity are mathematical facts of [[lem-sr-phase-rate-along-worldline]]; their identification with this ideal receiver's reading is the assumption adopted here. This is the pointwise equivalence to the momentarily comoving inertial phase receiver, together with the proper-time clock convention of [[post-sr-ideal-clocks-and-light]]. Reception comparisons use one and the same affine wave and events joined by one of its radial rays. This assumption does not postulate an emitter mechanism.

The instantaneous quantity may vary along an accelerated worldline. It is not an assertion that an observer's entire proper-time signal is monochromatic or that an arbitrary finite-duration Fourier measurement equals this value. For possible finite-apparatus use, define the local wavelength $\lambda_{\rm loc}:=2\pi c/\omega$ and the translational acceleration length $L_\alpha:=c^2/\alpha$, where $\alpha$ is the observer's proper-acceleration magnitude; for this congruence $L_\alpha=\rho$. The intended local ray regime has $\lambda_{\rm loc}/L_\alpha\ll1$ throughout the observation segment, receiver size small relative to $L_\alpha$, and an observation duration long enough for several cycles but short relative to $L_\alpha/c$. These qualitative scale separations give no numerical tolerance or measured uncertainty. The equality above is exact only inside the adopted ideal model; no accuracy claim for a real receiver follows from it.

This supplements, without changing, the accelerated-reception exclusion in [[post-sr-ideal-plane-wave-model]] (iv). It includes no detector dynamics, intensity, polarization, finite-bandwidth pulse or envelope, medium, dispersion, absorption, quantum or gravity model, no energy identification with $\hbar\omega$, and no empirical outcome or proof of the model's applicability. It is a sourced adopted idealization, not a deductive or experimentally established law.

derivations.claim: Put $\theta=aT/c$. The exponential definitions [F11] give $x^1+x^0=\rho e^\theta$ and $x^1-x^0=\rho e^{-\theta}$, both positive, so the image lies in $W$. Conversely, [F3] supplies the unique smooth Rindler inverse $\rho=\sqrt{(x^1)^2-(x^0)^2}$, $\theta=\frac12\log((x^1+x^0)/(x^1-x^0))$; setting $T=c\theta/a$ gives the stated inverse, which is smooth because $a,c>0$. The range agrees with [F3], and units and coordinates are those of [F1, F2].

$$T^*Q=\coprod_{q\in Q}T_q^*Q,\qquad \pi:T^*Q\to Q,\quad \pi(q,p)=q,$$

with the canonical smooth structure and induced cotangent charts supplied by the manifold construction in [[def-tautological-one-form-on-a-cotangent-bundle]]. The **tautological one-form** is $\theta_{(q,p)}(\xi)=p(d\pi_{(q,p)}\xi)$, and the **canonical cotangent two-form** is $\omega=-d\theta$. The exact theorem [[thm-the-canonical-cotangent-two-form-is-symplectic]] makes $(T^*Q,\omega)$ a symplectic manifold in the sense of [[def-symplectic-form-and-symplectic-manifold]]. We call this pair the **cotangent phase space** of $Q$.

In an induced chart $(q^1,\ldots,q^n,p_1,\ldots,p_n)$, $\theta=p_i\,dq^i$ and $\omega=dq^i\wedge dp_i$. A mathematical **observable** on this phase space means a smooth function $F:T^*Q\to\mathbb R$; this definition does not assert that a measurement has been performed or that every such function is physically measurable.

For an interpreted particle model, assign coordinates $q^i$ their declared units and assign the conjugate covector components $p_i$ units of action divided by the units of $q^i$. Thus $\theta$ and $\omega$ have action units, conventionally joule-seconds, and a bracket of quantities with units \([F]\) and \([G]\) has units \([F][G]/(\text{action})\). These are dimensional interpretations of the model, not additional mathematical premises. The use of $\mathrm{AC}_{\omega}$ is exactly the use in the smooth cotangent-bundle suppliers; no full Axiom of Choice is used.

$$C:=\{z\in U:\chi_1(z)=\cdots=\chi_r(z)=0\}$$

when $d\chi_1(z),\ldots,d\chi_r(z)$ are linearly independent at every $z\in C$. $$H_T(t,z):=H_c(t,z)+\sum_{a=1}^r u^a(t)\chi_a(z).$$

The functions $u^a$ are independent parameter functions; the definition does not assert that their equations determine them. If $H_c$ is an energy and $\chi_a$ has units \([\chi_a]\), then $u^a$ has units energy divided by \([\chi_a]\), so every term in $H_T$ has the same units. A later constraint, if generated by consistency, is not declared primary by this definition.

Use the signature $(-,+,+,+)$ throughout. In the flat case, **Minkowski spacetime** means the affine model $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ of [[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]: $A$ is an affine space, $\eta$ is a nondegenerate Lorentz form on its four-dimensional displacement space, and $C^+$ selects the future cone. In the curved case, a **background spacetime** means a prescribed smooth time-oriented Lorentzian four-manifold $(M,g,N)$ of [[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]; the metric and time orientation are fixed data, not dynamical unknowns here. No field equation or completeness assumption is included.

A **massive worldline** on an open interval $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ is a $C^2$ curve $x:I\to M$ with future-directed timelike tangent $T=dx/ds$ at every parameter value. This is the smooth subclass of [[def-gr-timelike-worldline-and-proper-time]]. A **null worldline** is a $C^2$ curve with nonzero future-directed null tangent everywhere. Its tangent has no proper-time normalization: $g(T,T)=0$, so the massive proper-time formula does not apply. In the flat model these are affine curves into $A$ with tangent in the selected future timelike or null cone from [[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]].

An **observer at an event** $p\in M$ is a future unit timelike vector $n\in T_pM$ with $g_p(n,n)=-1$, as in [[def-gr-observer-and-rest-space]]. Its instantaneous rest space is $n^\perp=\{v:g_p(v,n)=0\}$. This is a pointwise vector-space construction; the definition does not assign a clock reading or a moving frame to a lone observer.

An **observer congruence** on an open set $U\subseteq M$ is a smooth field of future unit timelike vectors on $U$, as in [[def-gr-observer-congruence-and-adapted-charts]]; its observer curves are its integral curves. A **tetrad** is a chosen orthonormal frame field, as in [[def-gr-local-frame-and-tetrad-fields]]. A **chart** is a coordinate map; an adapted chart is a chart whose spatial coordinates are constant along the congruence's integral curves. These objects are distinct: a chart need not be inertial, a tetrad need not be coordinate induced, and a congruence is a field of observers rather than a chart or a frame. This distinction agrees with [[def-sr-chart-tetrad-and-congruence-distinction]].

The coordinates and units used later are SI: in an inertial chart $x^0=ct$ and $x^i$ are metres, $t$ is seconds, $c>0$ is metres per second, and proper time is measured in seconds. In a general chart, coordinate components inherit their coordinate units; invariant equations are tensorial. No global inertial chart, global tetrad, or global observer congruence is asserted to exist.

$$v^iL_{v^i}=L,\qquad L_{v^iv^j}v^i=0,\qquad E_L:=v^iL_{v^i}-L=0.$$

Consequently the velocity Hessian is singular and the fibre derivative cannot be a local diffeomorphism there; a regular Legendre equivalence theorem cannot be applied. These conclusions do not imply that the motion is static or that the Lagrangian has a specified constraint surface.

Let $(M,g,T)$ be a smooth time-oriented Lorentzian four-manifold, $m>0$, and $L(x,V)=-mc\sqrt{-g(V,V)}$ on the future timelike tangent cone. Its fibre derivative is

$$p_a=mc\frac{g_{ab}V^b}{s},\qquad s=\sqrt{-g(V,V)}>0.$$

The velocity Hessian is $mc(g_{ab}/s+V_aV_b/s^3)$, has kernel exactly $\mathbb RV$, and rank three. The image consists exactly of the future shell $\Sigma_m^+=\{(x,p)\in T^*M:g_x^{-1}(p,p)=-m^2c^2,\ p^\sharp\text{ future}\}$. Each fibre is a connected positive ray, and the Legendre map is a surjective submersion onto this embedded image. Its energy $p(V)-L$ is zero; the map has no local inverse in the four-velocity direction.

In affine Minkowski space with $x^0=ct$, let $m\ge0$, $p_i$ be spatial momentum components and $p_i\ne0$ for $m=0$. On the future shell, $p_0=-E/c$, where

$$E(\mathbf p)=\sqrt{m^2c^4+c^2|\mathbf p|^2}.$$

On any compact interval $J=[t_1,t_2]$ of inertial time, the gauge $x^0=ct$ reduces the first-order shell action to

$$I_J=\int_{t_1}^{t_2}\left(p_i\dot q^i-E(\mathbf p)\right)dt,\qquad q^i=x^i.$$

The gauge pair $C_m=0$, $\psi=x^0-ct=0$ is second class because $\{C_m,\psi\}=-P^0\ne0$ on the future shell; its Dirac reduction gives the canonical spatial bracket. The reduced Hamilton equations are $\dot q^i=c^2p_i/E$, $\dot p_i=0$, agreeing with the unreduced characteristic trajectories. On this full flat future shell every characteristic line meets each inertial-time slice once; this global assertion does not extend by this proof to a curved temporal chart.

citations.quote:
Adopt the postulates [[post-gr-spacetime-and-classical-domain]],
[[post-gr-field-and-matter-assumptions]],
[[post-gr-einstein-field-law]] and
[[post-gr-ideal-clocks-and-free-fall]] of the classical gravitational
framework, with the field law in its direct-equation presentation and the unit
conventions of [[def-gr-si-unit-and-coordinate-conventions]]. Let
$(M,g,N)$ be the Schwarzschild exterior datum of mass parameter $m_*>0$ with
Schwarzschild radius $s=2G_Nm_*/c^2$ and static congruence
$n=f^{-1/2}\partial_0$, $f(r)=1-s/r$
([[def-gr-schwarzschild-exterior-model]]), and let the model's stress-energy
tensor be the vacuum prescription

$$T:=0\qquad\text{on }M,\qquad \Lambda:=0 .$$

Then all statements below are conditional deductions inside the model so
specified; they assert nothing about nature.

**(a) The Schwarzschild vacuum model.** $(M,g,N)$ satisfies the spacetime
postulate, $T=0$ is a smooth symmetric stress-energy tensor field on the
matter domain $M$ in the sense of [[def-gr-stress-energy-tensor-field]], the
prescription is admissible, and the adopted field law
$G_{ab}+\Lambda g_{ab}=\kappa T_{ab}$ holds identically on $M$. A **vacuum solution with zero cosmological parameter** here means
precisely a datum satisfying that equation with $T=0$ and $\Lambda=0$;
this datum is such a solution, read as a model of the framework. The model is not locally flat: its curvature tensor is nowhere
zero, while its Ricci tensor and Einstein tensor vanish identically
([[lem-gr-schwarzschild-ricci-and-einstein-tensors]] clause (d)).

**(b) Static clock readings.** The integral curves of $n$ are the static
observer worldlines at constant radius $r_0$
([[lem-gr-schwarzschild-static-congruence-and-clock-rates]] clause (b));
adopting the clock rule of [[post-gr-ideal-clocks-and-free-fall]] clause (i),
the reading difference of an ideal clock carried along such a worldline
between two events whose coordinate times differ by $\Delta t$ is

$$\Delta\tau=\sqrt{f(r_0)}\,\Delta t=\sqrt{1-\frac{s}{r_0}}\;\Delta t,$$

so two static clocks at radii $r_1,r_2$ compared over the same coordinate
interval with $\Delta t\ne0$ satisfy $\Delta\tau_1/\Delta\tau_2=\sqrt{f(r_1)/f(r_2)}$. The static
worldlines are not geodesics: their acceleration is
$a=\frac{s}{2r^2}\partial_r\ne0$, so the model assigns them to accelerated
(constrained) bodies and not to freely falling ones.

**(c) The mass parameter.** The parameter $m_*$ enters the model only through
$s=2G_Nm_*/c^2$ and through the quantities below; the framework reads $m_*$ as
the mass parameter of the model in kilograms
([[def-gr-si-unit-and-coordinate-conventions]] clause (a),
[[def-gr-schwarzschild-exterior-model]] clause (a)):

1. Let $\gamma:I\to M$ be a smooth future timelike geodesic, parametrized
   by proper time $\tau$ on an interval with nonempty interior, with
   $r\circ\gamma\equiv r_0>\frac{3s}{2}$. Put $\sigma:=\iota\circ\gamma:I\to S^2$
   and $t:=(x^0\circ\gamma)/c$. Its **angular speed with respect to $t$** is
   $\Omega:=\sqrt{\gamma_{S^2}(d\sigma/dt,d\sigma/dt)}$, where
   $d\sigma/dt:=\sigma'(\tau)/t'(\tau)$ and $t'(\tau)>0$ by future
   timelikeness. It has units $\mathrm s^{-1}$ and satisfies
   $\Omega^2=G_Nm_*/r_0^3$ in every angular orientation. For an equatorial
   curve, $\vartheta=\pi/2$ and $\Omega^2=(d\varphi/dt)^2$ in local polar
   charts ([[lem-gr-schwarzschild-circular-orbits-and-photon-sphere]]
   clause (a) and proof step 2.2). This is the Kepler-like law in which
   $m_*$ plays the role of the central mass;
2. in the isotropic chart of
   [[lem-gr-schwarzschild-isotropic-coordinate-form]], with
   $a=s/(4\rho)$, the exact identity
   $g_{00}+1=1-\bigl((1-a)/(1+a)\bigr)^2=4a/(1+a)^2$ gives
   $$g_{00}+1=+\frac{s}{\rho}+O(\rho^{-2})=+\frac{2G_Nm_*}{c^2\rho}+O(\rho^{-2}).$$
   Under the weak-field convention $g_{00}=-(1+2\Phi/c^2)$ to leading order
   ([[def-gr-stationary-weak-field-data]]), this is the coefficient
   $-2\Phi_N/c^2$ for the explicit exterior Newtonian potential
   $\Phi_N(\rho):=-G_Nm_*/\rho$ in the comparison reading of
   [[def-gr-newtonian-comparison-model-and-identification]].

The reading is a statement about the model's own identities and the adopted
unit and weak-field conventions; no numerical value of $G_N$ or $m_*$, no
Newtonian source model realized by matter and no comparison with any reported
mass is asserted.

**(d) Scope.** The model is an idealized vacuum model of the framework, not a
claim about the actual universe: no observation, apparatus, calibration or
uncertainty is used, and no comparison with data is made. The datum solves the
field law with the chosen parameters $(m_*,\Lambda,T)=(m_*,0,0)$; other
solutions of the same field law exist and are not excluded, and the exterior
domain $r>s$ contains no horizon or interior region, whose treatment is the
subject of the extension and Kruskal items of this page. The physical
interpretation of coordinates, clocks and bodies remains the adopted one of
the cited postulates.

Adopt as physical assumptions of the classical gravitational framework, in
addition to [[post-gr-spacetime-and-classical-domain]] and the matter-content
assumptions of the framework, the following rules by which ideal clocks, test
bodies and light couple to the metric $g$ of
[[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]].

**(i) Ideal clocks.** An **ideal clock** is an idealized physical device
carried along a future timelike worldline ([[def-gr-timelike-worldline-and-proper-time]])
whose readings are assumed to reproduce the proper time of that worldline:
the difference of two readings taken at two events of the worldline is the
proper-time increment between those events as defined by the metric, and it is
independent of the construction of the clock. Two ideal clocks moving along
the same worldline differ only by an additive constant (their choice of zero);
different worldlines generally accrue different proper times between the same
pair of events. The physical constant $c$ and the unit of duration are those
of [[def-gr-si-unit-and-coordinate-conventions]].

**(ii) Free fall of massive test bodies.** A **test body** is an uncharged
idealized body whose internal structure is small compared with the scale over
which the geometry of the model varies and whose gravitational self-field is
negligible within the model. An **ideal freely falling massive test body** is
assumed to have a worldline that is a future timelike geodesic of the
metric-selected connection ([[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]],
[[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]],
[[def-geodesic-of-an-affine-connection]]), traversed with physical
four-velocity $U=d\gamma/d\tau$ satisfying
$g_{\gamma(\tau)}(U,U)=-c^2$; proper time is an affine parameter of the
worldline ([[lem-gr-proper-time-reparametrization-and-four-velocity]]). The
worldline is determined by the event at which the body is released together
with its four-velocity there, by the uniqueness of the geodesic initial-value
problem ([[thm-gr-local-geodesics-and-exponential-map]]); no force, charge, or
rest mass of the body enters this rule.

**(iii) Light rays.** In the geometric-optics approximation an **ideal light
ray** propagating in the model is assumed to be a future null geodesic of the
metric-selected connection
([[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]],
[[def-geodesic-of-an-affine-connection]]). A null worldline carries no proper
time and no four-velocity in the sense of
[[def-gr-timelike-worldline-and-proper-time]]; within the approximation the
propagation of an ideal ray is independent of its frequency, and only the
ray's direction in the tangent space is fixed, not a scale along it.

**(iv) Scope and exclusions.** The three rules are adopted in the test-field
regime of the smooth classical model: the clocks, bodies and rays do not
back-react on the geometry, and the geometry varies smoothly on the scales
relevant to them. Configurations requiring the body's own gravitational field,
radiation reaction, an electromagnetic or other self-force, finite-size or
tidal couplings beyond the test-body idealization, non-geometric-optics
propagation, dispersion or dissipation of light, or quantum effects are
outside these assumptions and require additional model content. The
assumptions do not assert that any real clock, body or light ray is exactly
ideal, nor do they attach measured readings to any model.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be the Schwarzschild exterior datum with $s>0$ and
$f(r)=1-s/r$ ([[def-gr-schwarzschild-exterior-model]]), with
metric-selected connection $\nabla$. Let $\gamma:I\to M$ be a **future
timelike geodesic**, parametrized by proper time $\tau$, with tangent
$U=\gamma'$, so that $g(U,U)=-c^2$ and $U$ is future-directed
([[def-geodesic-of-an-affine-connection]],
[[lem-gr-parallel-transport-and-geodesic-speed]] clause 3,
[[def-gr-timelike-worldline-and-proper-time]]). Fix a spherical-polar product chart
$(x^0,r,\vartheta,\varphi)$ containing the image of $\gamma$ and write a dot
for $\frac{d}{d\tau}$. Define

$$e:=-g(U,\partial_0)=f\dot x^0,\qquad \ell:=g(U,\partial_\varphi)=r^2\sin^2\vartheta\,\dot\varphi .$$

Then:

**(a) Conserved quantities.** $\partial_0$ and $\partial_\varphi$ are Killing
fields of $g$, and $e$ and $\ell$ are constant along $\gamma$; moreover
$e>0$.

**(b) Equatorial reduction.** Suppose $\vartheta(\tau_0)=\frac{\pi}{2}$ and
$\dot\vartheta(\tau_0)=0$ at some $\tau_0\in I$. Then
$\vartheta(\tau)=\frac{\pi}{2}$ for all $\tau\in I$; the geodesic is
**equatorial**.

**(c) Radial reduction.** If $\gamma$ is equatorial, define the **effective
potential**

$$W_\ell(r):=f(r)\Bigl(c^2+\frac{\ell^2}{r^2}\Bigr).$$

Then the normalization identity

$$\dot r^2=e^2-W_\ell(r)$$

holds at every $\tau\in I$, and, given this identity, the $r$-component of the
geodesic equation is equivalent to the one-dimensional equation

$$\ddot r=-\frac12 W_\ell'(r),\qquad W_\ell'(r)=f'(r)\Bigl(c^2+\frac{\ell^2}{r^2}\Bigr)-2f(r)\frac{\ell^2}{r^3}.$$

**(d) Scope.** The reduction is local: it is stated on the interval $I$ on
which the geodesic stays in one product chart with $r>s$ and
$0<\vartheta<\pi$; no completeness, no extension of $\gamma$ beyond $I$, and
no statement about null geodesics is made. The quantities $e$ and $\ell$ are
constants of the given geodesic, not functions of the model.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be the Schwarzschild exterior datum with $s>0$ and
$f(r)=1-s/r$ ([[def-gr-schwarzschild-exterior-model]]), with
$f'=s/r^2$. Then:

For arbitrary $x^0_0,\varphi_0\in\mathbb R$, put
$\omega_0=(\cos\varphi_0,\sin\varphi_0,0)\in S^2$. For $\alpha\in\mathbb R$
define the rotation
$$R_\alpha(y_1,y_2,y_3):=(y_1\cos\alpha-y_2\sin\alpha,\ y_1\sin\alpha+y_2\cos\alpha,\ y_3),$$
and the global axial vector field $\Phi(y_1,y_2,y_3):=(-y_2,y_1,0)$ on $S^2$;
it is tangent because $y\cdot\Phi(y)=0$ for $y\in S^2$.
In every spherical-polar chart near the equator, $\Phi=\partial_\varphi$;
longitude expressions below are local chart expressions for the global sphere
curve $R_\alpha\omega_0$.

In this item, a **timelike circular geodesic** means a future timelike
geodesic whose areal radius $r$ is constant on an interval of positive length;
its angular orientation is unrestricted.

**(a) Existence of circular timelike geodesics.** Let $r_0>3s/2$ and choose
$\ell\in\mathbb R$ with

$$\ell^2=\frac{c^2sr_0^2}{2r_0-3s}>0,\qquad e:=\Bigl(f(r_0)\Bigl(c^2+\frac{\ell^2}{r_0^2}\Bigr)\Bigr)^{1/2} =\frac{c(r_0-s)\sqrt 2}{\sqrt{r_0(2r_0-3s)}}>0 .$$

Then the globally defined curve $\gamma:\mathbb R\to M$ is

$$\gamma(\tau):=\bigl(x^0_0+\tfrac{e}{f(r_0)}\tau,\ r_0,\ R_{\ell\tau/r_0^2}\omega_0\bigr).$$
In each local polar chart along it, $\vartheta=\pi/2$ and the longitude is
$\varphi_0+\ell\tau/r_0^2$ up to a constant multiple of $2\pi$.

It is a future timelike geodesic of the datum, with $g(\gamma',\gamma')=-c^2$
and with the conserved quantities $e=-g(\gamma',\partial_0)$ and
$\ell=g(\gamma',\Phi)$ of
[[lem-gr-schwarzschild-timelike-geodesic-reduction]]; it is a **circular
orbit** at radius $r_0$. Its angular velocity in the coordinate $x^0$ is

$$\frac{d\varphi}{dx^0}=\frac{\ell f(r_0)}{r_0^2e}=\operatorname{sgn}(\ell)\Bigl(\frac{s}{2r_0^3}\Bigr)^{1/2},\qquad\text{so}\qquad \Bigl(\frac{d\varphi}{dt}\Bigr)^2=\frac{G_Nm_*}{r_0^3},$$

$t=x^0/c$.

**(b) The circular-orbit condition is necessary.** Conversely, if
$\gamma:I\to M$ is any future timelike geodesic parametrized by proper time with
$r(\tau)\equiv r_0>s$ constant on an interval of positive length, then
$r_0>\frac{3s}{2}$. If $\gamma$ is equatorial, its conserved angular
momentum additionally satisfies $\ell^2=\dfrac{c^2sr_0^2}{2r_0-3s}$.
Consequently no timelike circular geodesic, in any angular orientation, exists
with $s<r_0\le\frac{3s}{2}$.

**(c) Stability threshold of the radial potential.** For each radius
$r>\frac{3s}{2}$ set $\ell_r^2:=c^2sr^2/(2r-3s)$ and regard $\ell_r$ as a
constant in the function $V_{\ell_r}(x):=\tfrac12 f(x)(c^2+\ell_r^2/x^2)$.
Differentiate with respect to $x$ at fixed $\ell_r$, then evaluate at $x=r$.
The result, evaluated at the circular value $\ell_r$, is

$$V_{\ell_r}''(r)=\frac{c^2s(r-3s)}{r^3(2r-3s)},\qquad r>\frac{3s}{2},$$

so $V_\ell$ has a strict local minimum at the circular-orbit radius exactly
for $r>3s$, a strict local maximum exactly for $\frac{3s}{2}<r<3s$, and
$V_\ell''(3s)=0$; the radius $r=3s$ is the **innermost stable circular orbit
radius** of the restricted model in this potential sense.

**(d) The photon sphere at $r=3s/2$.** Let $\ell\neq0$ and put
$r_0=\frac{3s}{2}$ and $e_0:=\dfrac{\lvert\ell\rvert\sqrt{f(r_0)}}{r_0}=\dfrac{2\lvert\ell\rvert}{3\sqrt3\,s}>0$.
Then the globally defined curve
$$\eta(\tau):=\bigl(x^0_0+\tfrac{e_0}{f(r_0)}\tau,\ r_0,\ R_{\ell\tau/r_0^2}\omega_0\bigr),\qquad \tau\in\mathbb R,$$
whose local polar expressions have $\vartheta=\pi/2$ and longitude
$\varphi_0+\ell\tau/r_0^2$ up to chart shifts, is a future null geodesic (a
**null circular orbit** or **photon sphere**
orbit) with conserved quantities $e_0=-g(\eta',\partial_0)$ and
$\ell=g(\eta',\Phi)$, and its angular velocity is

$$\frac{d\varphi}{dx^0}=\frac{\ell f(r_0)}{r_0^2e_0}=\operatorname{sgn}(\ell)\,\frac{\sqrt{f(r_0)}}{r_0},\qquad \Bigl(\frac{d\varphi}{dx^0}\Bigr)^2=\frac{f(r_0)}{r_0^2}=\frac{4}{27s^2}.$$

The **null effective potential** $W^{\mathrm n}_\ell(r):=f(r)\ell^2/r^2$
satisfies $(W^{\mathrm n}_\ell)'(3s/2)=0$ and
$(W^{\mathrm n}_\ell)''(3s/2)=-\dfrac{32\ell^2}{81s^4}<0$, so the photon-sphere
radius is a strict local maximum of the null potential.

**(e) Scope.** All statements are exact data of the restricted model: the
orbits are ideal geodesics of the metric on the exterior domain, the
stability claim is the sign of the second derivative of the stated potential,
and no claim is made about nonlinear stability, about orbital decay, about
observations or about the interior region. The case $r_0=s$ is excluded, and
the reduction is stated only where $r>s$.

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and let $F:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be a map. Consider the autonomous first-order system

$$z'(t)=F(z(t)),$$

read as the first-order system of [[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]] with $D=\mathbb R\times U$ and right-hand side $(t,z)\mapsto F(z)$. A **solution** below means a solution of this system on an interval containing $0$; a solution whose interval is $[0,\infty)$ or contains it is said to be **defined for all $t\ge0$**.

A solution $\tilde z:J\to U$ **extends** $z:I\to U$ when $I\subseteq J$ and $\tilde z|_I=z$; the extension is proper if $I\subsetneq J$. A solution is **maximal** when it has no proper extension ([[def-maximal-ode-solution]]). All stability predicates below quantify over maximal solutions whose intervals contain $0$; their local restrictions remain solutions. This convention asserts neither existence nor uniqueness of maximal solutions for an arbitrary map $F$.

A point $z_*\in U$ is an **equilibrium** (also **fixed point** or **zero**) of $F$ when $F(z_*)=0$; then the constant function $z(t)=z_*$ is a solution on every interval containing $0$.

Let $z_*\in U$ be an equilibrium.

1. $z_*$ is **Lyapunov stable** (or simply **stable**) when for every Euclidean ball $B_\varepsilon(z_*)$ with $\overline{B_\varepsilon(z_*)}\subseteq U$ ([[def-metric-ball]]) there is $\delta\in(0,\varepsilon]$ such that every maximal solution $z$ with $\|z(0)-z_*\|_2<\delta$ ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]) is defined for all $t\ge0$ and satisfies

$$\|z(t)-z_*\|_2<\varepsilon\qquad(t\ge0).$$

2. $z_*$ is **asymptotically stable** when it is Lyapunov stable and in addition there is $\delta_0>0$ such that every maximal solution $z$ with $\|z(0)-z_*\|_2<\delta_0$ is defined for all $t\ge0$ and satisfies $\|z(t)-z_*\|_2\to0$ as $t\to\infty$.

An equilibrium which is not Lyapunov stable is **unstable**. An equilibrium is **globally asymptotically stable** when it is asymptotically stable and every maximal solution of the system is defined for all $t\ge0$ and converges to it as $t\to\infty$.

Let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $F:D\to\mathbb R^n$ be continuous and locally Lipschitz in the state variable, and let $(t_0,x_0)\in D$. Then a unique local solution of the IVP exists on some interval around the initial time. More quantitatively, if $h,r>0$ make

$$[t_0-h,t_0+h]\times\overline B(x_0,r)\subseteq D,$$

if $\|F\|_2\le M$ and $F$ has state-Lipschitz constant $L$ on this cylinder, and if $hM\le r$ and $Lh<1$, then there is exactly one solution on $[t_0-h,t_0+h]$ through $(t_0,x_0)$ whose graph lies in the cylinder. Any two solutions through the same initial data agree on every common subinterval containing $t_0$.

In particular, a unique local solution exists on an interval around the initial time.

Let $n\ge1$, let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$ be open, and let $F:D\to\mathbb R^n$ be continuous and locally Lipschitz in the state variable, locally uniformly in time, in the sense of [[def-locally-lipschitz-in-the-state-variable]]. Let $t_0<b$ be reals, let $x_0\in\mathbb R^n$ with $(t_0,x_0)\in D$, and let $x:[t_0,b)\to\mathbb R^n$ be a solution of the initial value problem

$$x'(t)=F\bigl(t,x(t)\bigr),\qquad x(t_0)=x_0$$

on $[t_0,b)$ ([[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]]). Suppose there is a compact set $K\subseteq D$ and a real $\delta>0$ such that

$$\bigl(t,x(t)\bigr)\in K\qquad\text{for every }t\in(b-\delta,b)\cap[t_0,b).$$

Then:

1. there is $\varepsilon>0$ and a solution $\tilde x:[t_0,b+\varepsilon)\to\mathbb R^n$ of the same initial value problem with $\tilde x(t)=x(t)$ for all $t\in[t_0,b)$; in particular $\tilde x(b)=\lim_{t\uparrow b}x(t)$ exists and lies in the state projection of $K$;
2. if moreover $D=\mathbb R\times U$ for an open $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ and $F$ is autonomous, $F(t,z)=G(z)$ with $G:U\to\mathbb R^n$ continuous and locally Lipschitz in the state variable ([[def-locally-lipschitz-in-the-state-variable]]), and if there is a compact $K_0\subseteq U$ with $x(t)\in K_0$ for every $t\in(b-\delta,b)\cap[t_0,b)$, then the extension conclusion of clause 1 holds as well.

derivations.claim: By [F1], the reduced vector field is $F_\ell(r,w)=(w,-W_\ell'(r)/2)$ on the open set $(s,\infty)\times\mathbb R$. It is smooth there and [F4] gives a unique local solution through every state. Differentiating $W_\ell=f(c^2+\ell^2/r^2)$ gives $W_\ell'=c^2s/r^2-2\ell^2/r^3+3s\ell^2/r^4$; substituting the circular value of $\ell^2$ from [F2] yields $W_\ell'(r_c)=0$, so $F_\ell(r_c,0)=0$. Along every solution, $H_\ell(r,w):=\tfrac12(w^2+W_\ell(r))$ satisfies $dH_\ell/d\tau=w(-W_\ell'/2)+(W_\ell'/2)w=0$. Thus $H_\ell$ is constant on each solution interval.

Suppose $r_c>3s$. By [F2], $W_\ell''(r_c)>0$, so continuity gives an interval about $r_c$ on which $W_\ell''>0$. Since $W_\ell'(r_c)=0$, the derivative is negative to the left and positive to the right there; hence $W_\ell$ has a strict local minimum. Fix any phase-space radius $\varepsilon>0$ whose closed ball about $z_c$ lies in $(s,\infty)\times\mathbb R$. Choose $0<\eta<\varepsilon/2$ so $[r_c-\eta, r_c+\eta]\subset(s,\infty)$ and both boundary values of $W_\ell$ exceed $W_\ell(r_c)$. By continuity of $H_\ell$, choose $0<\delta\le\varepsilon$ so every state within $\delta$ of $z_c$ has $|r-r_c|<\eta/2$, energy below both boundary potential halves, and $H_\ell-W_\ell(r_c)/2<\varepsilon^2/8$. Conservation in 1.1 prevents such a solution from reaching either radial boundary, since there $H_\ell\ge W_\ell(r_c\pm\eta)/2$. Inside the resulting radial interval $W_\ell(r)\ge W_\ell(r_c)$, so $w^2/2=H_\ell-W_\ell(r)/2<\varepsilon^2/8$ and $|w|<\varepsilon/2$. The state stays in a compact subset of the open domain; [F5] rules out a finite forward maximal endpoint. With $|r-r_c|<\eta<\varepsilon/2$ and $|w|<\varepsilon/2$, it remains inside the prescribed phase-space ball for every $\tau\ge0$. This is Lyapunov stability by [F3].

Suppose $3s/2<r_c<3s$. By [F2], $W_\ell''(r_c)<0$; shrink $\eta>0$ so $W_\ell'(r)<0$ on $(r_c,r_c+\eta]$. For any proposed initial-state radius $\delta>0$, choose $r_0\in(r_c,r_c+\min\{\eta/2,\delta/2\})$ and initial data $(r_0,0)$. [F4] supplies a local solution. Its acceleration is $-W_\ell'(r_0)/2>0$, and conservation of $H_\ell$ gives, on the outgoing branch, $w=\sqrt{W_\ell(r_0)-W_\ell(r)}$. The solution reaches $r_c+\eta$ in finite time: the travel-time integral is $\int_{r_0}^{r_c+\eta}[W_\ell(r_0)-W_\ell(r)]^{-1/2}dr$, whose only endpoint singularity is bounded by a constant times $(r-r_0)^{-1/2}$ because $W_\ell'(r_0)<0$. Hence initial data arbitrarily close to $z_c$ leave the fixed neighborhood of radius $\eta$, contradicting [F3].

At $r_c=3s$, the circular relation gives $\ell^2=3c^2s^2$. Differentiating $W_\ell(r)=c^2(1-s/r)+\ell^2(r^{-2}-sr^{-3})$ at this fixed $\ell$ gives $W_\ell'(r)=c^2s(r-3s)^2/r^4$ and $W_\ell''(r)=-2c^2s(r-3s)(r-6s)/r^5$. Thus $W_\ell'$ is positive except at $3s$ and $W_\ell''$ changes sign there, so the equilibrium is a stationary inflection. Fix $0<\eta<s$ and, for any $\delta>0$, choose $r_0\in(3s-\min\{\eta/2,\delta/2\},3s)$ with initial data $(r_0,0)$. [F4] supplies a local solution. The acceleration is negative. On the inward branch energy conservation yields $w=-\sqrt{W_\ell(r_0)-W_\ell(r)}$ for $3s-\eta\le r<r_0$, since $W_\ell$ is strictly increasing on that interval. The travel-time integral to $3s-\eta$ is finite; near $r_0$ its integrand is bounded by a constant times $(r_0-r)^{-1/2}$ because $W_\ell'(r_0)>0$. Thus arbitrarily close initial data leave the fixed neighborhood of radius $\eta$, so [F3] says the equilibrium is not Lyapunov stable.

The two subcritical cases in 2.2–2.3 are not Lyapunov stable, while the supercritical case in 2.1 is Lyapunov stable. These are deductions under the adopted Schwarzschild free-fall model [A1] and concern only its fixed-angular-momentum radial subsystem.
