citations.quote:
Adopt the postulates [[post-gr-spacetime-and-classical-domain]],
[[post-gr-field-and-matter-assumptions]],
[[post-gr-einstein-field-law]] and
[[post-gr-ideal-clocks-and-free-fall]] of the classical gravitational
framework, with the field law in its direct-equation presentation and the unit
conventions of [[def-gr-si-unit-and-coordinate-conventions]]. Let
$(M,g,N)$ be the Schwarzschild exterior datum of mass parameter $m_*>0$ with
Schwarzschild radius $s=2G_Nm_*/c^2$ and static congruence
$n=f^{-1/2}\partial_0$, $f(r)=1-s/r$
([[def-gr-schwarzschild-exterior-model]]), and let the model's stress-energy
tensor be the vacuum prescription

$$T:=0\qquad\text{on }M,\qquad \Lambda:=0 .$$

Then all statements below are conditional deductions inside the model so
specified; they assert nothing about nature.

**(a) The Schwarzschild vacuum model.** $(M,g,N)$ satisfies the spacetime
postulate, $T=0$ is a smooth symmetric stress-energy tensor field on the
matter domain $M$ in the sense of [[def-gr-stress-energy-tensor-field]], the
prescription is admissible, and the adopted field law
$G_{ab}+\Lambda g_{ab}=\kappa T_{ab}$ holds identically on $M$. A **vacuum solution with zero cosmological parameter** here means
precisely a datum satisfying that equation with $T=0$ and $\Lambda=0$;
this datum is such a solution, read as a model of the framework. The model is not locally flat: its curvature tensor is nowhere
zero, while its Ricci tensor and Einstein tensor vanish identically
([[lem-gr-schwarzschild-ricci-and-einstein-tensors]] clause (d)).

**(b) Static clock readings.** The integral curves of $n$ are the static
observer worldlines at constant radius $r_0$
([[lem-gr-schwarzschild-static-congruence-and-clock-rates]] clause (b));
adopting the clock rule of [[post-gr-ideal-clocks-and-free-fall]] clause (i),
the reading difference of an ideal clock carried along such a worldline
between two events whose coordinate times differ by $\Delta t$ is

$$\Delta\tau=\sqrt{f(r_0)}\,\Delta t=\sqrt{1-\frac{s}{r_0}}\;\Delta t,$$

so two static clocks at radii $r_1,r_2$ compared over the same coordinate
interval with $\Delta t\ne0$ satisfy $\Delta\tau_1/\Delta\tau_2=\sqrt{f(r_1)/f(r_2)}$. The static
worldlines are not geodesics: their acceleration is
$a=\frac{s}{2r^2}\partial_r\ne0$, so the model assigns them to accelerated
(constrained) bodies and not to freely falling ones.

**(c) The mass parameter.** The parameter $m_*$ enters the model only through
$s=2G_Nm_*/c^2$ and through the quantities below; the framework reads $m_*$ as
the mass parameter of the model in kilograms
([[def-gr-si-unit-and-coordinate-conventions]] clause (a),
[[def-gr-schwarzschild-exterior-model]] clause (a)):

1. Let $\gamma:I\to M$ be a smooth future timelike geodesic, parametrized
   by proper time $\tau$ on an interval with nonempty interior, with
   $r\circ\gamma\equiv r_0>\frac{3s}{2}$. Put $\sigma:=\iota\circ\gamma:I\to S^2$
   and $t:=(x^0\circ\gamma)/c$. Its **angular speed with respect to $t$** is
   $\Omega:=\sqrt{\gamma_{S^2}(d\sigma/dt,d\sigma/dt)}$, where
   $d\sigma/dt:=\sigma'(\tau)/t'(\tau)$ and $t'(\tau)>0$ by future
   timelikeness. It has units $\mathrm s^{-1}$ and satisfies
   $\Omega^2=G_Nm_*/r_0^3$ in every angular orientation. For an equatorial
   curve, $\vartheta=\pi/2$ and $\Omega^2=(d\varphi/dt)^2$ in local polar
   charts ([[lem-gr-schwarzschild-circular-orbits-and-photon-sphere]]
   clause (a) and proof step 2.2). This is the Kepler-like law in which
   $m_*$ plays the role of the central mass;
2. in the isotropic chart of
   [[lem-gr-schwarzschild-isotropic-coordinate-form]], with
   $a=s/(4\rho)$, the exact identity
   $g_{00}+1=1-\bigl((1-a)/(1+a)\bigr)^2=4a/(1+a)^2$ gives
   $$g_{00}+1=+\frac{s}{\rho}+O(\rho^{-2})=+\frac{2G_Nm_*}{c^2\rho}+O(\rho^{-2}).$$
   Under the weak-field convention $g_{00}=-(1+2\Phi/c^2)$ to leading order
   ([[def-gr-stationary-weak-field-data]]), this is the coefficient
   $-2\Phi_N/c^2$ for the explicit exterior Newtonian potential
   $\Phi_N(\rho):=-G_Nm_*/\rho$ in the comparison reading of
   [[def-gr-newtonian-comparison-model-and-identification]].

The reading is a statement about the model's own identities and the adopted
unit and weak-field conventions; no numerical value of $G_N$ or $m_*$, no
Newtonian source model realized by matter and no comparison with any reported
mass is asserted.

**(d) Scope.** The model is an idealized vacuum model of the framework, not a
claim about the actual universe: no observation, apparatus, calibration or
uncertainty is used, and no comparison with data is made. The datum solves the
field law with the chosen parameters $(m_*,\Lambda,T)=(m_*,0,0)$; other
solutions of the same field law exist and are not excluded, and the exterior
domain $r>s$ contains no horizon or interior region, whose treatment is the
subject of the extension and Kruskal items of this page. The physical
interpretation of coordinates, clocks and bodies remains the adopted one of
the cited postulates.

Adopt as physical assumptions of the classical gravitational framework, in
addition to [[post-gr-spacetime-and-classical-domain]] and the matter-content
assumptions of the framework, the following rules by which ideal clocks, test
bodies and light couple to the metric $g$ of
[[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]].

**(i) Ideal clocks.** An **ideal clock** is an idealized physical device
carried along a future timelike worldline ([[def-gr-timelike-worldline-and-proper-time]])
whose readings are assumed to reproduce the proper time of that worldline:
the difference of two readings taken at two events of the worldline is the
proper-time increment between those events as defined by the metric, and it is
independent of the construction of the clock. Two ideal clocks moving along
the same worldline differ only by an additive constant (their choice of zero);
different worldlines generally accrue different proper times between the same
pair of events. The physical constant $c$ and the unit of duration are those
of [[def-gr-si-unit-and-coordinate-conventions]].

**(ii) Free fall of massive test bodies.** A **test body** is an uncharged
idealized body whose internal structure is small compared with the scale over
which the geometry of the model varies and whose gravitational self-field is
negligible within the model. An **ideal freely falling massive test body** is
assumed to have a worldline that is a future timelike geodesic of the
metric-selected connection ([[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]],
[[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]],
[[def-geodesic-of-an-affine-connection]]), traversed with physical
four-velocity $U=d\gamma/d\tau$ satisfying
$g_{\gamma(\tau)}(U,U)=-c^2$; proper time is an affine parameter of the
worldline ([[lem-gr-proper-time-reparametrization-and-four-velocity]]). The
worldline is determined by the event at which the body is released together
with its four-velocity there, by the uniqueness of the geodesic initial-value
problem ([[thm-gr-local-geodesics-and-exponential-map]]); no force, charge, or
rest mass of the body enters this rule.

**(iii) Light rays.** In the geometric-optics approximation an **ideal light
ray** propagating in the model is assumed to be a future null geodesic of the
metric-selected connection
([[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]],
[[def-geodesic-of-an-affine-connection]]). A null worldline carries no proper
time and no four-velocity in the sense of
[[def-gr-timelike-worldline-and-proper-time]]; within the approximation the
propagation of an ideal ray is independent of its frequency, and only the
ray's direction in the tangent space is fixed, not a scale along it.

**(iv) Scope and exclusions.** The three rules are adopted in the test-field
regime of the smooth classical model: the clocks, bodies and rays do not
back-react on the geometry, and the geometry varies smoothly on the scales
relevant to them. Configurations requiring the body's own gravitational field,
radiation reaction, an electromagnetic or other self-force, finite-size or
tidal couplings beyond the test-body idealization, non-geometric-optics
propagation, dispersion or dissipation of light, or quantum effects are
outside these assumptions and require additional model content. The
assumptions do not assert that any real clock, body or light ray is exactly
ideal, nor do they attach measured readings to any model.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be the Schwarzschild exterior datum with $s>0$ and $f(r)=1-s/r$ on $r>s$. Let $\gamma(\lambda)$ be an affinely parametrized null geodesic of its metric-selected connection whose image lies in the equatorial plane $\vartheta=\pi/2$, and choose the orientation so that

$$E:=f(r)\frac{dx^0}{d\lambda}>0,\qquad L:=r^2\frac{d\varphi}{d\lambda}\ge0.$$

Both quantities are constant along $\gamma$. With impact parameter $b:=L/E\ge0$ and $H(r):=f(r)/r^2$, its radial equation is

$$\left(\frac{dr}{d\lambda}\right)^2=E^2\bigl(1-b^2H(r)\bigr).$$

Moreover, $H'(r)=(3s-2r)/r^4$, so $H$ has its unique exterior maximum at $r_{\rm ph}=3s/2$, with $H(r_{\rm ph})=4/(27s^2)$. Thus the critical impact parameter for a radial turning point is $b_{\rm c}=3\sqrt3\,s/2$.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold and let
$\nabla$ be its metric-selected connection, whose existence and uniqueness are
supplied by [[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]]; its
Christoffel symbols are the smooth chart functions of
[[def-christoffel-symbols-of-an-affine-connection]]. Recall that a **geodesic**
is a curve with $D_t\gamma'=0$ in its parameter
([[def-geodesic-of-an-affine-connection]],
[[def-covariant-derivative-along-a-curve]]).

**(a) Local existence, uniqueness and maximality.** For every $(p,v)\in TM$
there is a unique maximal geodesic $\gamma_{p,v}:I_{p,v}\to M$ with
$\gamma_{p,v}(0)=p$ and $\gamma_{p,v}'(0)=v$; its domain $I_{p,v}$ is an open
interval containing $0$ and is not asserted to be all of $\mathbb R$.

**(b) Smooth dependence.** The set
$\mathcal G:=\{(t,p,v):t\in I_{p,v}\}\subseteq\mathbb R\times TM$ is open, and
the evaluation map $(t,p,v)\mapsto\gamma_{p,v}(t)$ is smooth on $\mathcal G$.

**(c) Scaling.** For every $s\in\mathbb R$ and every $t\in\mathbb R$,
$t\in I_{p,sv}$ if and only if $st\in I_{p,v}$, and then
$\gamma_{p,sv}(t)=\gamma_{p,v}(st)$.

**(d) The exponential map.** Define $\mathcal E_p:=\{v\in T_pM:1\in I_{p,v}\}$
and $\exp_p:\mathcal E_p\to M$, $\exp_p(v):=\gamma_{p,v}(1)$, and let
$\psi_p:T_pM\to\mathbb R^4$ be the coordinate isomorphism of a basis
$e_0,\dots,e_3$ of $T_pM$. Then $\mathcal E_p$ is open and star-shaped about
$0$ (if $v\in\mathcal E_p$ and $0\le s\le1$, then $sv\in\mathcal E_p$),
$\exp_p$ is smooth, $\exp_p(0)=p$, and, under the canonical identification
$T_0(T_pM)\cong T_pM$ induced by the chart $\psi_p$ on $T_pM$,
$$d(\exp_p)_0=\operatorname{id}_{T_pM}.$$
Consequently there is a star-shaped open neighborhood $W_p\subseteq\mathcal E_p$
of $0$ such that $\exp_p|_{W_p}$ is a diffeomorphism onto an open subset of
$M$.

Let $n\ge1$, let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$ be open, and let $F:D\to\mathbb R^n$ be continuous and locally Lipschitz in the state variable, locally uniformly in time, in the sense of [[def-locally-lipschitz-in-the-state-variable]]. Let $t_0<b$ be reals, let $x_0\in\mathbb R^n$ with $(t_0,x_0)\in D$, and let $x:[t_0,b)\to\mathbb R^n$ be a solution of the initial value problem

$$x'(t)=F\bigl(t,x(t)\bigr),\qquad x(t_0)=x_0$$

on $[t_0,b)$ ([[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]]). Suppose there is a compact set $K\subseteq D$ and a real $\delta>0$ such that

$$\bigl(t,x(t)\bigr)\in K\qquad\text{for every }t\in(b-\delta,b)\cap[t_0,b).$$

Then:

1. there is $\varepsilon>0$ and a solution $\tilde x:[t_0,b+\varepsilon)\to\mathbb R^n$ of the same initial value problem with $\tilde x(t)=x(t)$ for all $t\in[t_0,b)$; in particular $\tilde x(b)=\lim_{t\uparrow b}x(t)$ exists and lies in the state projection of $K$;
2. if moreover $D=\mathbb R\times U$ for an open $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ and $F$ is autonomous, $F(t,z)=G(z)$ with $G:U\to\mathbb R^n$ continuous and locally Lipschitz in the state variable ([[def-locally-lipschitz-in-the-state-variable]]), and if there is a compact $K_0\subseteq U$ with $x(t)\in K_0$ for every $t\in(b-\delta,b)\cap[t_0,b)$, then the extension conclusion of clause 1 holds as well.

This item assumes the axiom of countable choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ through
the tangent-bundle convention of [[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]
clause (c); the product-smooth-structure supplier has no choice hypothesis
([[def-countable-choice]]); no further choice principle is used.

**(a) Parameters.** Let $c>0$, $G_N>0$ and $m_*>0$ be the constants and mass
parameter of the Schwarzschild exterior datum, and put
$s:=2G_Nm_*/c^2>0$ ([[def-gr-schwarzschild-exterior-model]] clause (a)). The
**Kruskal model datum of mass parameter $m_*$** is constructed from these
data as follows.

**(b) Domain and smooth structure.** Let
$\Omega:=\{(U,V)\in\mathbb R^2:UV<1\}$ and let
$\mathcal K:=\Omega\times S^2$, where $S^2\subset\mathbb R^3$ is the unit
Euclidean sphere, with the product smooth structure
([[prop-products-of-smooth-manifolds-have-a-canonical-product-smooth-structure]],
[[def-euclidean-spheres-and-closed-balls]]). It is a smooth four-manifold
without boundary. Write $U,V:\mathcal K\to\mathbb R$ for the first two
projections and $\iota:\mathcal K\to S^2$ for the third. A **Kruskal product
chart** uses any smooth chart on $S^2$. In a spherical-polar Kruskal chart the
angular coordinates satisfy $0<\vartheta<\pi$ and
$\gamma_{S^2}=\operatorname{diag}(1,\sin^2\vartheta)_{ij}$; these charts omit
the two poles, which are covered by ordinary sphere charts.

**(c) The radial function.** The datum carries a function
$r:\mathcal K\to(0,\infty)$, the **Kruskal radial function**, characterized by
the implicit relation

$$U\,V=-\Bigl(\frac{r}{s}-1\Bigr)e^{r/s}\qquad\text{at every point of }\mathcal K .$$

That for every $(U,V)\in\Omega$ there is exactly one $r(U,V)>0$ satisfying
this relation, and that $r$ is smooth, is not asserted here; it is proved in
[[lem-gr-kruskal-model-properties]] on this page, the justification record of
this definition. The value $r=0$ is not attained on $\mathcal K$, and
$r=s$ exactly on the axes $U=0$ or $V=0$.

**(d) The metric.** Define the metric globally by

$$g_{\mathcal K}=-\frac{2s^3}{r}e^{-r/s}(dU\otimes dV+dV\otimes dU)+r^2\,\iota^*\gamma_{S^2}.$$

In every spherical-polar Kruskal chart its component functions are

$$g_{UV}:=g_{VU}:=-\frac{2s^3}{r}e^{-r/s},\qquad g_{\vartheta\vartheta}:=r^2,\qquad g_{\varphi\varphi}:=r^2\sin^2\vartheta,\qquad g_{UU}:=g_{VV}:=g_{U\vartheta}:=g_{U\varphi}:=g_{V\vartheta}:=g_{V\varphi}:=0,$$

where $r$ is the function of clause (c) evaluated at the point. This global
expression defines a smooth symmetric covariant $2$-tensor field on
$\mathcal K$ once the smoothness of $r$ is established by
[[lem-gr-kruskal-model-properties]]. In another sphere chart the angular block
is $r^2(\gamma_{ij})$. That $g_{\mathcal K}$ is Lorentzian is proved, not
asserted, in the same lemma.

**(e) Time orientation.** Define the field
$N_{\mathcal K}:=\partial_U+\partial_V$ on $\mathcal K$. Its component
expression is the same in every Kruskal chart; that it is a smooth timelike
field and hence a time orientation of $g_{\mathcal K}$ is proved in
[[lem-gr-kruskal-model-properties]].

**(f) Scope.** The datum is a geometric object: the definition asserts
nothing about whether $g_{\mathcal K}$ satisfies any field equation, about
its causal structure, about the maximality of the extension it provides, or
about nature. The comparison with the exterior datum, the vacuum property and
the causal structure are the content of the two following items on this page.
The region $\{UV=1\}$, where the implicit relation of clause (c) has no
solution with $r>0$, is not part of $\mathcal K$ and is not appended to it by
this definition.

Let $(\mathcal K,r,g_{\mathcal K},N_{\mathcal K})$ be the Kruskal model datum of
mass parameter $m_*>0$ with Schwarzschild radius $s=2G_Nm_*/c^2>0$
([[def-gr-kruskal-model-data]], [[lem-gr-kruskal-model-properties]]), let
$(U,V,\xi^2,\xi^3)$ be any Kruskal product chart, and let $\gamma_{ij}$ be
the round-sphere components in its angular chart. In a spherical-polar
Kruskal chart, $(\xi^2,\xi^3)=(\vartheta,\varphi)$ and
$\gamma_{ij}=\operatorname{diag}(1,\sin^2\vartheta)$. Define
$A:\mathcal K\to(0,\infty)$ by

$$A:=\frac{4s^3e^{-r/s}}{r},$$

so that in a product chart $g_{UV}=g_{VU}=-A/2$, $g_{ij}=r^2\gamma_{ij}$ and
the mixed base-angular components vanish. In a spherical-polar chart this
reads $g_{\vartheta\vartheta}=r^2$,
$g_{\varphi\varphi}=r^2\sin^2\vartheta$. For a
$C^1$ curve $\eta:J\to\mathcal K$ with $J$ a nonempty interval write
$\dot\eta=(\dot U,\dot V,\dot\xi^2,\dot\xi^3)$ for its coordinate
components, and call $\eta$ **future-directed causal** when
$g_{\mathcal K}(\dot\eta,\dot\eta)\le0$ and
$g_{\mathcal K}(\dot\eta,N_{\mathcal K})<0$ at every parameter value. Then:

**(a) Causal cone criterion.** At every $p\in\mathcal K$ and for every
$X\in T_p\mathcal K$ with chart components $(X^U,X^V,X^\omega)$ one has:
$X$ is causal and future-directed if and only if

$$X^U\ge0,\qquad X^V\ge0,\qquad X^U+X^V>0,\qquad A(p)\,X^UX^V\ \ge\ r(p)^2\,\gamma_p(X^\omega,X^\omega),$$

where $\gamma_p(X^\omega,X^\omega)$ is the round-sphere squared norm of the
angular part. In particular every future-directed causal tangent has both
$X^U\ge0$ and $X^V\ge0$.

**(b) Monotonicity.** Along every future-directed causal $C^1$ curve the
functions $U$ and $V$ are nondecreasing, and along every past-directed causal
$C^1$ curve (where $g(\dot\eta,\dot\eta)\le0$ and
$g(\dot\eta,N_{\mathcal K})>0$) they are nonincreasing.

**(c) Radial null geodesics and their affine parameters.** For every
$(U_0,V_0,\omega_0)\in\mathcal K$ there is a unique maximal solution
$\lambda\mapsto(U(\lambda),V_0,\omega_0)$ of
$\dfrac{dU}{d\lambda}=\dfrac{1}{A(U(\lambda),V_0)}$, $U(0)=U_0$; it is an
affinely parametrized null geodesic of $g_{\mathcal K}$ with
$g(\dot\eta,\dot\eta)=0$. The same holds for
$\lambda\mapsto(U_0,V(\lambda),\omega_0)$ with
$\dfrac{dV}{d\lambda}=\dfrac{1}{A(U_0,V(\lambda))}$. Both are
future-directed, and $\lambda$ increases strictly with $U$, respectively with
$V$, because $A>0$. Moreover $\partial_U r=-\dfrac{s^2Ve^{-r/s}}{r}$ and
$\partial_Vr=-\dfrac{s^2Ue^{-r/s}}{r}$ at every point of $\mathcal K$.

**(d) Escape horizon.** Call a future-directed causal $C^1$ curve $\eta$
**escaping to the right exterior** when there is a parameter value after which
$\eta$ stays in the open quadrant $\{U<0,\ V>0\}$ and
$r(\eta(t))\to+\infty$ as $t\to+\infty$ (a point with $U\ge0$ cannot reach the
quadrant $\{U<0,V>0\}$ at all, by (b), and this is the sense in which the
horizon is a one-way membrane here). Then:

1. no future-directed causal curve issued at a point $p$ with $U(p)\ge0$
   escapes to the right exterior;
2. every point $p$ with $U(p)<0$ admits such a curve: for
   $t>0$ the curve $\eta_p(t):=(U(p),\,V(p)+t,\,\omega(p))$ is a future-directed
   null $C^1$ curve, it stays in
   $\{U<0,V>0\}$ for $t>1+|V(p)|$ and satisfies
   $r(\eta_p(t))\to+\infty$ as $t\to+\infty$.

Consequently the exact nonescaping set of the datum is $\{U\ge0\}$ with
boundary the null surface $\{U=0\}$, and the past-directed dual statement
singles out $\{V=0\}$ as the boundary of the region admitting past-directed
escape to the right exterior: here escape means eventual residence in
$\{U<0,V>0\}$ with $r\to+\infty$ as the past-directed parameter tends to
$+\infty$.

**(e) Decreasing areal radius.** If $U(p)>0$ and $V(p)>0$, then along both
future directions of the radial null geodesics of (c) through $p$ the function
$r$ is strictly decreasing as their affine parameter $\lambda$ increases:
on $\lambda\mapsto(U_0,V(\lambda),\omega_0)$ and on
$\lambda\mapsto(U(\lambda),V_0,\omega_0)$.

**(f) Scope.** All statements are geometric properties of the smooth Kruskal
datum on $\mathcal K$; no maximality, geodesic completeness or uniqueness is
claimed, the set $\{UV=1\}$ (where $r=0$) is not part of $\mathcal K$, and no
statement is made about the physical interpretation of any curve. The escape
notion of (d) is defined by the displayed conditions on $U,V$ and $r$ and does
not presuppose a conformal infinity.

derivations.claim: Choose $R>r_{\rm ph}$ so $b^2H(R)<1$. At $r=R$, set $\theta=\pi/2$, $\dot x^0=E/f(R)$, $\dot r=-E\sqrt{1-b^2H(R)}$, $\dot\theta=0$, and $\dot\varphi=L/R^2$. The null condition in [F1] is satisfied, the tangent is future directed because $\dot x^0>0$, and [F2] gives a local geodesic. On the past branch $\dot r\to-E$ as $r\to\infty$, so $\int_R^\infty dr/[E\sqrt{1-b^2H(r)}]=\infty$; compact continuation on finite radial intervals supplies an incoming ray from infinity for every $b\ge0$.

By [F1], $H$ increases on $(s,r_{\rm ph})$, decreases on $(r_{\rm ph},\infty)$, and vanishes at both exterior ends. If $b>b_{\rm c}$, then $b^2H(r_{\rm ph})>1$, so there is one root $r_-\in(s,r_{\rm ph})$ and one simple outer root $r_*>r_{\rm ph}$. The affine time from any finite large radius to $r_*$ is finite because near the simple root $[E\sqrt{1-b^2H(r)}]^{-1}=O((r-r_*)^{-1/2})$.

If $b=b_{\rm c}$, direct factorization gives $1-b_{\rm c}^2H(r)=(2r-3s)^2(r+3s)/(4r^3)$. The incoming radial speed vanishes linearly as $r\downarrow r_{\rm ph}$; hence the affine integral diverges like $\int dr/(r-r_{\rm ph})$. The angular integrand has the same simple-pole behavior, so the ray approaches the photon sphere only at infinite affine parameter and accumulates logarithmically divergent azimuth.

If $0\le b<b_{\rm c}$, then $b^2H(r)<1$ for every $r>s$ by [F1]. The inward branch has no turning point and reaches the exterior boundary $r=s$ in finite affine parameter because $1-b^2H(r)\to1$ there. The exterior calculation ends at that boundary. If a future continuation is placed in the Kruskal model and enters $U\ge0$, [F3] prevents it from returning to the right exterior.

For $b>b_{\rm c}$, [F2] extends the incoming ray through the outer turn: the radial first integral gives $\ddot r=-E^2b^2H'(r)/2>0$ at $r_*$, so it leaves with $\dot r>0$. On every finite segment with $r\ge r_*$, the conserved quantities bound $|\dot r|$, $|\dot x^0|=E/f(r)$ and $|\dot\varphi|=L/r^2$; the state stays in a compact subset of the smooth exterior tangent domain and cannot end at a finite affine parameter. On the outgoing branch $\dot r\to E>0$, while $|\dot r|\le E$, so it reaches arbitrarily large radii only at infinite affine parameter. Also $|d\varphi/dr|=b/[r^2\sqrt{1-b^2H(r)}]$ is $O((r-r_*)^{-1/2})$ at the turn and $O(r^{-2})$ at infinity; integrating both halves gives the convergent formula in clause 1.

The simple outer root, critical double root and no-turn regimes in 2.1–2.3 give all three clauses. Only the last clause uses the separate Kruskal continuation, and no observation or apparatus model is used.

boundaries.evidence: The statement assumes s>0 and the exterior has radii r>s; step 1.1 constructs an incoming ray at a finite R.
Clause 3 includes b=0; step 2.3 proves finite-affine boundary arrival for this radial case as well.

boundaries.reason: The statement has no one-element, unit-object, or single-component normalization case.

Steps 2.1–3.1 check turning, horizon-boundary, and infinity integral endpoints explicitly.
Step 1.1 constructs null initial data explicitly and uses local existence; no choice axiom is invoked.

The statement is not an if-and-only-if claim, so there is no reverse direction to verify.

citations.quote:
Adopt the postulates [[post-gr-spacetime-and-classical-domain]],
[[post-gr-field-and-matter-assumptions]],
[[post-gr-einstein-field-law]] and
[[post-gr-ideal-clocks-and-free-fall]] of the classical gravitational
framework, with the field law in its direct-equation presentation and the unit
conventions of [[def-gr-si-unit-and-coordinate-conventions]]. Let
$(M,g,N)$ be the Schwarzschild exterior datum of mass parameter $m_*>0$ with
Schwarzschild radius $s=2G_Nm_*/c^2$ and static congruence
$n=f^{-1/2}\partial_0$, $f(r)=1-s/r$
([[def-gr-schwarzschild-exterior-model]]), and let the model's stress-energy
tensor be the vacuum prescription

$$T:=0\qquad\text{on }M,\qquad \Lambda:=0 .$$

Then all statements below are conditional deductions inside the model so
specified; they assert nothing about nature.

**(a) The Schwarzschild vacuum model.** $(M,g,N)$ satisfies the spacetime
postulate, $T=0$ is a smooth symmetric stress-energy tensor field on the
matter domain $M$ in the sense of [[def-gr-stress-energy-tensor-field]], the
prescription is admissible, and the adopted field law
$G_{ab}+\Lambda g_{ab}=\kappa T_{ab}$ holds identically on $M$. A **vacuum solution with zero cosmological parameter** here means
precisely a datum satisfying that equation with $T=0$ and $\Lambda=0$;
this datum is such a solution, read as a model of the framework. The model is not locally flat: its curvature tensor is nowhere
zero, while its Ricci tensor and Einstein tensor vanish identically
([[lem-gr-schwarzschild-ricci-and-einstein-tensors]] clause (d)).

**(b) Static clock readings.** The integral curves of $n$ are the static
observer worldlines at constant radius $r_0$
([[lem-gr-schwarzschild-static-congruence-and-clock-rates]] clause (b));
adopting the clock rule of [[post-gr-ideal-clocks-and-free-fall]] clause (i),
the reading difference of an ideal clock carried along such a worldline
between two events whose coordinate times differ by $\Delta t$ is

$$\Delta\tau=\sqrt{f(r_0)}\,\Delta t=\sqrt{1-\frac{s}{r_0}}\;\Delta t,$$

so two static clocks at radii $r_1,r_2$ compared over the same coordinate
interval with $\Delta t\ne0$ satisfy $\Delta\tau_1/\Delta\tau_2=\sqrt{f(r_1)/f(r_2)}$. The static
worldlines are not geodesics: their acceleration is
$a=\frac{s}{2r^2}\partial_r\ne0$, so the model assigns them to accelerated
(constrained) bodies and not to freely falling ones.

**(c) The mass parameter.** The parameter $m_*$ enters the model only through
$s=2G_Nm_*/c^2$ and through the quantities below; the framework reads $m_*$ as
the mass parameter of the model in kilograms
([[def-gr-si-unit-and-coordinate-conventions]] clause (a),
[[def-gr-schwarzschild-exterior-model]] clause (a)):

1. Let $\gamma:I\to M$ be a smooth future timelike geodesic, parametrized
   by proper time $\tau$ on an interval with nonempty interior, with
   $r\circ\gamma\equiv r_0>\frac{3s}{2}$. Put $\sigma:=\iota\circ\gamma:I\to S^2$
   and $t:=(x^0\circ\gamma)/c$. Its **angular speed with respect to $t$** is
   $\Omega:=\sqrt{\gamma_{S^2}(d\sigma/dt,d\sigma/dt)}$, where
   $d\sigma/dt:=\sigma'(\tau)/t'(\tau)$ and $t'(\tau)>0$ by future
   timelikeness. It has units $\mathrm s^{-1}$ and satisfies
   $\Omega^2=G_Nm_*/r_0^3$ in every angular orientation. For an equatorial
   curve, $\vartheta=\pi/2$ and $\Omega^2=(d\varphi/dt)^2$ in local polar
   charts ([[lem-gr-schwarzschild-circular-orbits-and-photon-sphere]]
   clause (a) and proof step 2.2). This is the Kepler-like law in which
   $m_*$ plays the role of the central mass;
2. in the isotropic chart of
   [[lem-gr-schwarzschild-isotropic-coordinate-form]], with
   $a=s/(4\rho)$, the exact identity
   $g_{00}+1=1-\bigl((1-a)/(1+a)\bigr)^2=4a/(1+a)^2$ gives
   $$g_{00}+1=+\frac{s}{\rho}+O(\rho^{-2})=+\frac{2G_Nm_*}{c^2\rho}+O(\rho^{-2}).$$
   Under the weak-field convention $g_{00}=-(1+2\Phi/c^2)$ to leading order
   ([[def-gr-stationary-weak-field-data]]), this is the coefficient
   $-2\Phi_N/c^2$ for the explicit exterior Newtonian potential
   $\Phi_N(\rho):=-G_Nm_*/\rho$ in the comparison reading of
   [[def-gr-newtonian-comparison-model-and-identification]].

The reading is a statement about the model's own identities and the adopted
unit and weak-field conventions; no numerical value of $G_N$ or $m_*$, no
Newtonian source model realized by matter and no comparison with any reported
mass is asserted.

**(d) Scope.** The model is an idealized vacuum model of the framework, not a
claim about the actual universe: no observation, apparatus, calibration or
uncertainty is used, and no comparison with data is made. The datum solves the
field law with the chosen parameters $(m_*,\Lambda,T)=(m_*,0,0)$; other
solutions of the same field law exist and are not excluded, and the exterior
domain $r>s$ contains no horizon or interior region, whose treatment is the
subject of the extension and Kruskal items of this page. The physical
interpretation of coordinates, clocks and bodies remains the adopted one of
the cited postulates.

Adopt as physical assumptions of the classical gravitational framework, in
addition to [[post-gr-spacetime-and-classical-domain]] and the matter-content
assumptions of the framework, the following rules by which ideal clocks, test
bodies and light couple to the metric $g$ of
[[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]].

**(i) Ideal clocks.** An **ideal clock** is an idealized physical device
carried along a future timelike worldline ([[def-gr-timelike-worldline-and-proper-time]])
whose readings are assumed to reproduce the proper time of that worldline:
the difference of two readings taken at two events of the worldline is the
proper-time increment between those events as defined by the metric, and it is
independent of the construction of the clock. Two ideal clocks moving along
the same worldline differ only by an additive constant (their choice of zero);
different worldlines generally accrue different proper times between the same
pair of events. The physical constant $c$ and the unit of duration are those
of [[def-gr-si-unit-and-coordinate-conventions]].

**(ii) Free fall of massive test bodies.** A **test body** is an uncharged
idealized body whose internal structure is small compared with the scale over
which the geometry of the model varies and whose gravitational self-field is
negligible within the model. An **ideal freely falling massive test body** is
assumed to have a worldline that is a future timelike geodesic of the
metric-selected connection ([[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]],
[[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]],
[[def-geodesic-of-an-affine-connection]]), traversed with physical
four-velocity $U=d\gamma/d\tau$ satisfying
$g_{\gamma(\tau)}(U,U)=-c^2$; proper time is an affine parameter of the
worldline ([[lem-gr-proper-time-reparametrization-and-four-velocity]]). The
worldline is determined by the event at which the body is released together
with its four-velocity there, by the uniqueness of the geodesic initial-value
problem ([[thm-gr-local-geodesics-and-exponential-map]]); no force, charge, or
rest mass of the body enters this rule.

**(iii) Light rays.** In the geometric-optics approximation an **ideal light
ray** propagating in the model is assumed to be a future null geodesic of the
metric-selected connection
([[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]],
[[def-geodesic-of-an-affine-connection]]). A null worldline carries no proper
time and no four-velocity in the sense of
[[def-gr-timelike-worldline-and-proper-time]]; within the approximation the
propagation of an ideal ray is independent of its frequency, and only the
ray's direction in the tangent space is fixed, not a scale along it.

**(iv) Scope and exclusions.** The three rules are adopted in the test-field
regime of the smooth classical model: the clocks, bodies and rays do not
back-react on the geometry, and the geometry varies smoothly on the scales
relevant to them. Configurations requiring the body's own gravitational field,
radiation reaction, an electromagnetic or other self-force, finite-size or
tidal couplings beyond the test-body idealization, non-geometric-optics
propagation, dispersion or dissipation of light, or quantum effects are
outside these assumptions and require additional model content. The
assumptions do not assert that any real clock, body or light ray is exactly
ideal, nor do they attach measured readings to any model.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be the Schwarzschild exterior datum of mass parameter $m_*$
with Schwarzschild radius $s>0$ and $f(r)=1-s/r$
([[def-gr-schwarzschild-exterior-model]]), with metric-selected connection
$\nabla$ ([[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]],
[[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]]). Define the
smooth vector field

$$n:=f^{-1/2}\,\partial_0=\Bigl(1-\frac{s}{r}\Bigr)^{-1/2}\partial_0$$

on $M$. Then:

**(a) Observer congruence.** $n$ is a smooth observer congruence on $M$ in the
sense of [[def-gr-observer-congruence-and-adapted-charts]]: $g(n,n)=-1$ and
$g(n,N)<0$ at every point, so $n$ is a future-directed unit timelike field.

**(b) Integral curves.** For any $p=(c_0,r_0,\omega_0)\in M$, including sphere poles, the maximal integral curve of $n$ through $p$, with length-valued flow parameter $\lambda\in\mathbb R$, is
$$\lambda\mapsto\bigl(c_0+f(r_0)^{-1/2}\lambda,\ r_0,\ \omega_0\bigr).$$
It is defined on all of $\mathbb R$ and is the **static observer worldline** at radius $r_0$. In a spherical-polar chart it has constant angular coordinates $(\vartheta_0,\varphi_0)$; in any angular chart the sphere point is constant, and the global coordinate $x^0$ increases monotonically.

**(c) Proper time and clock rate.** Along each static observer worldline the
proper time $\tau$ is an affine function of the flow parameter $\lambda$, with
$\frac{d\tau}{d\lambda}=\frac1c$, and

$$\Delta\tau=\frac{\sqrt{f(r_0)}}{c}\,\Delta x^0=\sqrt{f(r_0)}\,\Delta t,$$

where $\Delta x^0$ is the coordinate difference in metres between two events
of the worldline and $\Delta t=\Delta x^0/c$ is the same difference in
seconds. In particular the proper-time increment is strictly positive for
$\Delta x^0>0$, and it is smaller than $\Delta t$ for $\Delta x^0>0$ at every finite radius
because $0<f(r_0)<1$.

**(d) Clock-rate ratio.** For two static observers at radii
$r_1,r_2\in(s,\infty)$ compared over the same coordinate interval
$\Delta x^0\ne0$, the proper-time increments satisfy

$$\frac{\Delta\tau_1}{\Delta\tau_2}=\sqrt{\frac{f(r_1)}{f(r_2)}}=\sqrt{\frac{1-s/r_1}{1-s/r_2}} .$$

**(e) Acceleration.** The acceleration field of the congruence is
$a:=\nabla_nn=\frac{f'(r)}{2}\,\partial_1=\frac{s}{2r^2}\,\partial_r$; it is
spatial, nowhere zero, and points in the direction of increasing $r$, so the
static observers are not geodesics.

**(f) Scope.** These are identities of the geometric datum. The reading of
$\tau$ as the time measured by an ideal clock and of the congruence as a
family of static observers belongs to the framework's postulates and is not
asserted here; no measurement and no comparison with any observed rate is
made.

Adopt the Schwarzschild exterior vacuum model of
[[pthm-gr-schwarzschild-vacuum-model]]: the exterior datum $(M,g,N)$ of mass
parameter $m_*>0$ with $s=2G_Nm_*/c^2$ and $f(r)=1-s/r$
([[def-gr-schwarzschild-exterior-model]]), its metric-selected connection
$\nabla$ ([[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]],
[[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]]), its static
congruence $n=f^{-1/2}\partial_0$
([[lem-gr-schwarzschild-static-congruence-and-clock-rates]]), and the light-ray
rule that ideal light rays are future null geodesics of $\nabla$
([[post-gr-ideal-clocks-and-free-fall]] clause (iii)). Let $\eta:J\to M$ be
the specified ray, a smooth affinely parametrized geodesic of $\nabla$ on an
interval $J$, with tangent $W=\eta'$, $g(W,W)=0$ and $W$ future-directed
([[def-geodesic-of-an-affine-connection]],
[[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]]). Let
$\lambda_E,\lambda_R\in J$ with $\lambda_E<\lambda_R$ and suppose
$\eta(\lambda_E)$ and $\eta(\lambda_R)$ lie on static observer worldlines of
radii $r_E=r(\eta(\lambda_E))$ and $r_R=r(\eta(\lambda_R))$ with
$r_E,r_R\in(s,\infty)$. For each parameter value define the **observer energy
of the ray relative to the static observers** by

$$E(\lambda):=-c\,g_{\eta(\lambda)}\bigl(W(\lambda),n(\eta(\lambda))\bigr),$$

the value of the observer-energy definition of
[[def-gr-observer-relative-energy-and-momentum]] clause (a) for the unit
observer $n$. Then:

**(a) Constancy of the Killing pairing.** $K=\partial_0$ is a Killing field of
$g$ and the function $C(\lambda):=-g_{\eta(\lambda)}(W(\lambda),K(\eta(\lambda)))$
is constant along $J$;
moreover $C>0$.

**(b) The observer-energy ratio.** $E(\lambda)>0$ along the ray and

$$\frac{E(\lambda_R)}{E(\lambda_E)}=\sqrt{\frac{f(r_E)}{f(r_R)}}=\sqrt{\frac{1-s/r_E}{1-s/r_R}} .$$

**(c) Redshift parameter.** If the **redshift parameter** of the pair of events
is defined by $z:=\dfrac{E(\lambda_E)}{E(\lambda_R)}-1$, equivalently by
$1+z=E(\lambda_E)/E(\lambda_R)$, then

$$1+z=\sqrt{\frac{f(r_R)}{f(r_E)}} .$$

The ratio in (b) and (c) is unchanged if $W$ is replaced by $\mu W$ with a
positive constant $\mu$: a future null ray determines its future tangent only
up to positive scale,
and only the ratio of energies is asserted. No observed wavelength, spectral
line, calibration or measurement enters the statement; the identification of
the ratio with a frequency ratio of an ideal ray is part of the framework's
geometric-optics reading, and moving observers require additional factors.

**(d) Scope.** The statement is a model prediction for the specified ideal
ray and the specified static observers; it asserts no redshift measurement and
no property of any real source, and it excludes non-geometric-optics
propagation, dispersion and any apparatus or analysis model.

This item assumes the axiom of countable choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ through
the tangent-bundle structure used by
[[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]] clause (c)
([[def-countable-choice]]); no further choice principle is used.

**(a) Parameters and the Schwarzschild radius.** Let $c>0$ and $G_N>0$ be real
constants and let $m_*>0$ be a real **mass parameter**. Put

$$s:=\frac{2G_Nm_*}{c^2}>0 .$$

The number $s$ is the **Schwarzschild radius** of the datum. Neither $c$,
$G_N$ nor $m_*$ is measured here; the physical reading of $c$ and $G_N$ as the
framework's conversion and Newton constants and of $m_*$ as a mass is fixed by
the physical conventions of the framework, not by this definition.

**(b) The underlying manifold and its product charts.** Let $S^2:=S_2(0,1)=
\{y\in\mathbb R^3:\lVert y\rVert_2=1\}$ be the unit Euclidean sphere with the
subspace topology of [[def-euclidean-spheres-and-closed-balls]]. Specify its
smooth structure as the maximal atlas generated by the following two charts
([[def-smooth-manifold]]). For $\varepsilon\in\{+1,-1\}$ put
$p_\varepsilon=(0,0,\varepsilon)$ and
$U_\varepsilon=S^2\setminus\{p_\varepsilon\}$, and define

$$\sigma_\varepsilon:U_\varepsilon\to\mathbb R^2,\qquad \sigma_\varepsilon(y)=\frac{(y_1,y_2)}{1-\varepsilon y_3}.$$

These open domains cover $S^2$. Each chart is a homeomorphism onto
$\mathbb R^2$, with inverse, for $u=(u_1,u_2)$ and $q=u_1^2+u_2^2$,

$$\sigma_\varepsilon^{-1}(u)=\left(\frac{2u_1}{1+q},\frac{2u_2}{1+q},\varepsilon\frac{q-1}{1+q}\right).$$

The two inverse identities follow by substitution; all displayed denominators
are nonzero on their domains. On the overlap both transition maps are
$u\mapsto u/(u_1^2+u_2^2)$ on $\mathbb R^2\setminus\{0\}$, hence smooth.
The subspace is Hausdorff and has a countable basis given by intersections
with Euclidean balls of rational centres and positive rational radii.
Thus these charts specify a smooth two-manifold without boundary. This is
the standard sphere structure used for the round metric below: the inclusion
has the displayed smooth local parametrizations, and their differentials
are injective because composition with $\sigma_\varepsilon$ is the identity.
Let $M$ be the product manifold

$$M:=\mathbb R\times(s,\infty)\times S^2$$

with the product smooth structure
([[prop-products-of-smooth-manifolds-have-a-canonical-product-smooth-structure]]);
it is a smooth four-manifold without boundary. Write $x^0:M\to\mathbb R$ and
$r:M\to(s,\infty)$ for the first and second projections and $\iota:M\to S^2$
for the third. A **product chart** of $M$ is a smooth chart on the product
whose angular part is a smooth chart of $S^2$. In a **spherical-polar product
chart**, $0<\vartheta<\pi$ and the components of the round metric
$\gamma_{S^2}$ of [[ex-the-round-metric-on-the-sphere-as-an-induced-metric]]
are $\gamma_{22}=1$, $\gamma_{23}=\gamma_{32}=0$,
$\gamma_{33}=\sin^2\vartheta$. These polar charts omit the two poles; ordinary
smooth sphere charts around the poles complete the product atlas.

**(c) The metric.** Let $f:(s,\infty)\to(0,\infty)$ be the smooth function

$$f(r):=1-\frac{s}{r} .$$

Define $g$ globally by the coordinate-free expression

$$g=-f\,d(x^0)\otimes d(x^0)+f^{-1}\,dr\otimes dr+r^2\,\iota^*\gamma_{S^2}.$$

In every spherical-polar product chart its component functions are

$$g_{00}:=-f(r),\qquad g_{11}:=\frac{1}{f(r)},\qquad g_{22}:=r^2,\qquad g_{33}:=r^2\sin^2\vartheta,$$

and $g_{ab}:=0$ whenever $a\ne b$, $a,b\in\{0,1,2,3\}$, with the index order
$(x^0,x^1,x^2,x^3)=(x^0,r,\vartheta,\varphi)$. This is a smooth symmetric
covariant $2$-tensor field on all of $M$
([[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]]); the component display is local
to spherical-polar charts, and $f>0$ because $r>s$. The pair $(M,g)$ is the **Schwarzschild exterior
metric of mass parameter $m_*$**; the datum of this definition is the
quadruple $(c,G_N,m_*,g)$. With these parameters fixed, write $(M,g,N)$
for its associated geometric datum, with $N$ as in clause (d). The geometric
datum depends on the parameters only through $s$ and does not retain $c$,
$G_N$ and $m_*$ separately. That $(M,g,N)$ is a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold
of signature $(-,+,+,+)$ is not asserted here; it is proved in the companion metric-properties lemma of this page (its
justification record in the frontmatter), which also records the equivalent
coordinate-free description
$g=-f\,d(x^0)\otimes d(x^0)+f^{-1}\,dr\otimes dr+r^2\,\iota^*\gamma_{S^2}$.

**(d) Time orientation and the Schwarzschild chart.** The field
$N:=\partial_0$ is the smooth product vector field on $M$
([[def-derivation-at-a-point-and-tangent-space]]); the chart components of $g$
are independent of $x^0$, so $N$ is the restriction of a global vector field,
and $g(N,N)=-f(r)<0$ at every point. The datum carries the time orientation
$N$. Spherical-polar product charts are **Schwarzschild charts** of the datum;
at the poles the same metric is represented in the smooth sphere charts of
the product atlas. We write $t$ for the coordinate $x^0/c$ when the datum is
read in the framework's unit conventions.

**(e) Scope.** The domain of the datum is the exterior region $r>s$; the
definition asserts nothing about $r=s$, about $r\le 0$, about any matter, or
about any equation satisfied by $g$. The horizon $r=s$ is not part of the
datum, and a continuation of the metric to $r=s$ requires the separate constructions recorded on this page, the
regularity lemma for the advanced chart and the Kruskal model-properties
lemma. Whether the datum is a solution of the
framework's field law is proved, not defined, in the Ricci-and-Einstein-tensor lemma of this
page.

For $x>0$, define the **integral logarithm**

$$L(x):=\int_1^x\frac{dt}{t},$$

using the oriented integral when $x<1$
([[def-oriented-integral]]).

This is well defined. The function $t\mapsto1/t$ is continuous wherever
$t\neq0$ by the quotient clause of
[[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]]. For $x\neq1$ it is therefore continuous on the nondegenerate compact interval
with endpoints $1$ and $x$, hence Riemann integrable there by
[[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]], whose hypothesis is $a<b$. At $x=1$ the
interval is degenerate and that theorem does not apply; there
[[def-oriented-integral]] stipulates $\int_1^1f=0$, so $L(1)=0$ directly.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be integrable
([[def-darboux-integral]]), let $F$ be its integral function
([[def-the-integral-function]]), and let $c \in [a,b]$ be a point at which $f$ is
continuous ([[def-continuity-real]]). Then $F$ is differentiable at $c$ as a
function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]) and

$$F'(c) \;=\; f(c) .$$

At $c = a$ and $c = b$ this is the one-sided statement, which is what
[[def-derivative]] means at those points: every point of a nondegenerate interval
is a limit point of it, so $F'(c)$ is a meaningful symbol at every $c \in [a,b]$,
and the difference quotient is taken over $[a,b] \setminus \{c\}$.

**Consequently, if $f$ is continuous on the whole of $[a,b]$, then $F$ is a
primitive of $f$ there**: $F' = f$ at every point of $[a,b]$.

**Continuity at $c$ is a hypothesis and it cannot be dropped.** For an integrable
$f$ that is discontinuous at $c$, $F'(c)$ may fail to exist, and it may exist and
differ from $f(c)$; both are exhibited on the companion page, by
an integrable function with no primitive and by a false
statement about the integral function.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f, g : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be integrable
([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then:

1. **Nonnegativity.** If $f(x) \ge 0$ for every $x \in [a,b]$ then
   $\int_a^b f \ge 0$.
2. **Monotonicity.** If $f(x) \le g(x)$ for every $x \in [a,b]$ then
   $$\int_a^b f \;\le\; \int_a^b g .$$
3. **Two-sided bound.** If $m \le f(x) \le M$ for every $x \in [a,b]$, with
   $m, M$ real, then
   $$m\,(b-a) \;\le\; \int_a^b f \;\le\; M\,(b-a) .$$

**Equality in claim 1 does not force $f$ to vanish.** A nonnegative integrable
function with integral $0$ may be positive at infinitely many points; that is
[[fs-nonnegative-integrable-with-zero-integral-vanishes]] on the previous page's
companion. Under the additional hypothesis of continuity the conclusion does
hold, and that is [[thm-nonnegative-continuous-with-zero-integral-vanishes]]
below.

**Claim 2 is stated for $a < b$ and is not orientation-invariant.** With the
convention of [[def-oriented-integral]], $f \le g$ gives
$\int_u^v f \le \int_u^v g$ when $u \le v$ and the reverse inequality when
$u \ge v$, since both sides change sign together.

It is **almost regular on a declared domain $\mathcal D_0\subseteq\mathcal D$** when the following are all assumed: $\mathbb F L|_{\mathcal D_0}$ has constant rank; its image $N$ is an embedded submanifold of $\mathbb R\times T^*Q$; its corestriction $\mathcal D_0\to N$ is a surjective submersion (its differential is surjective at every point); and every fibre of that corestriction is connected. $$T^*Q=\coprod_{q\in Q}T_q^*Q,\qquad \pi:T^*Q\to Q,\quad \pi(q,p)=q,$$

with the canonical smooth structure and induced cotangent charts supplied by the manifold construction in [[def-tautological-one-form-on-a-cotangent-bundle]]. The **tautological one-form** is $\theta_{(q,p)}(\xi)=p(d\pi_{(q,p)}\xi)$, and the **canonical cotangent two-form** is $\omega=-d\theta$. The exact theorem [[thm-the-canonical-cotangent-two-form-is-symplectic]] makes $(T^*Q,\omega)$ a symplectic manifold in the sense of [[def-symplectic-form-and-symplectic-manifold]]. We call this pair the **cotangent phase space** of $Q$.

In an induced chart $(q^1,\ldots,q^n,p_1,\ldots,p_n)$, $\theta=p_i\,dq^i$ and $\omega=dq^i\wedge dp_i$. A mathematical **observable** on this phase space means a smooth function $F:T^*Q\to\mathbb R$; this definition does not assert that a measurement has been performed or that every such function is physically measurable.

For an interpreted particle model, assign coordinates $q^i$ their declared units and assign the conjugate covector components $p_i$ units of action divided by the units of $q^i$. Thus $\theta$ and $\omega$ have action units, conventionally joule-seconds, and a bracket of quantities with units \([F]\) and \([G]\) has units \([F][G]/(\text{action})\). These are dimensional interpretations of the model, not additional mathematical premises. $$C:=\{z\in U:\chi_1(z)=\cdots=\chi_r(z)=0\}$$

when $d\chi_1(z),\ldots,d\chi_r(z)$ are linearly independent at every $z\in C$. The regular-level theorem [[thm-a-regular-level-set-is-an-embedded-submanifold]] then gives $C$ its embedded-submanifold structure and $T_zC=\bigcap_a\ker d\chi_a(z)$. For functions $F,G$ on $U$, write $F\approx G$ when $F|_C=G|_C$; thus $F\approx0$ means that $F$ vanishes on $C$, without requiring it to vanish off $C$.

Given a smooth canonical Hamiltonian $H_c$ on $U$ and multiplier functions $u^a(t)$, the **total generator** is

$$H_T(t,z):=H_c(t,z)+\sum_{a=1}^r u^a(t)\chi_a(z).$$

The functions $u^a$ are independent parameter functions; the definition does not assert that their equations determine them. If $H_c$ is an energy and $\chi_a$ has units \([\chi_a]\), then $u^a$ has units energy divided by \([\chi_a]\), so every term in $H_T$ has the same units. A later constraint, if generated by consistency, is not declared primary by this definition.

Use the signature $(-,+,+,+)$ throughout. In the flat case, **Minkowski spacetime** means the affine model $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ of [[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]: $A$ is an affine space, $\eta$ is a nondegenerate Lorentz form on its four-dimensional displacement space, and $C^+$ selects the future cone. In the curved case, a **background spacetime** means a prescribed smooth time-oriented Lorentzian four-manifold $(M,g,N)$ of [[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]; the metric and time orientation are fixed data, not dynamical unknowns here. No field equation or completeness assumption is included.

A **massive worldline** on an open interval $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ is a $C^2$ curve $x:I\to M$ with future-directed timelike tangent $T=dx/ds$ at every parameter value. This is the smooth subclass of [[def-gr-timelike-worldline-and-proper-time]]. A **null worldline** is a $C^2$ curve with nonzero future-directed null tangent everywhere. Its tangent has no proper-time normalization: $g(T,T)=0$, so the massive proper-time formula does not apply. In the flat model these are affine curves into $A$ with tangent in the selected future timelike or null cone from [[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]].

An **observer at an event** $p\in M$ is a future unit timelike vector $n\in T_pM$ with $g_p(n,n)=-1$, as in [[def-gr-observer-and-rest-space]]. Its instantaneous rest space is $n^\perp=\{v:g_p(v,n)=0\}$. This is a pointwise vector-space construction; the definition does not assign a clock reading or a moving frame to a lone observer.

An **observer congruence** on an open set $U\subseteq M$ is a smooth field of future unit timelike vectors on $U$, as in [[def-gr-observer-congruence-and-adapted-charts]]; its observer curves are its integral curves. A **tetrad** is a chosen orthonormal frame field, as in [[def-gr-local-frame-and-tetrad-fields]]. A **chart** is a coordinate map; an adapted chart is a chart whose spatial coordinates are constant along the congruence's integral curves. These objects are distinct: a chart need not be inertial, a tetrad need not be coordinate induced, and a congruence is a field of observers rather than a chart or a frame. This distinction agrees with [[def-sr-chart-tetrad-and-congruence-distinction]].

The coordinates and units used later are SI: in an inertial chart $x^0=ct$ and $x^i$ are metres, $t$ is seconds, $c>0$ is metres per second, and proper time is measured in seconds. In a general chart, coordinate components inherit their coordinate units; invariant equations are tensorial. No global inertial chart, global tetrad, or global observer congruence is asserted to exist.
